Not an expert, so treat this as a hunch, but a few of us have poked at these enough
that I reckon I can picture what's actually going on, and I've not seen it spelled
out here yet.

I don't think it's the pairing or the network key that breaks. Both ends still have
the right key the whole time, which is why the wall switch and the relay carry on
working fine. What breaks is the frame counter.

Every encrypted Zigbee message has a number on it that only ever counts up. The
coordinator keeps track of the highest one it's seen from each device and bins
anything the same or lower, so nobody can record an old command and replay it later.
The device is meant to write that number to memory so it carries on from the right
place after a reboot.

My guess is this firmware doesn't save that number properly when the power drops. So
after a power cycle the device comes back thinking it's on a much lower number than
the coordinator last saw, everything it sends looks like an old replayed message, and
the coordinator throws it all away. The device is alive and talking, the coordinator
just ignores it.

That would explain the bits that don't otherwise add up. It runs happily for months
and only dies after a power cut, because that reboot is the one moment the counter
has to survive. A rejoin sorts it for an hour or so because re-pairing resets the
numbers on both sides, but it doesn't touch the actual save-on-power-loss problem, so
it comes straight back. And it fits why this is set off by flicking the power rather
than any particular HA update. My two both dropped within minutes of each other right
after I switched the lighting MCB off and back on.

Worth adding something on the "allow unsecured rejoins" workaround a few people are
running, because I think it fits the same picture.

Normally when the device tries to get back in after it's lost sync, the coordinator
refuses it, and that's the point where it just sits there unavailable. Turning on
unsecured rejoins basically props that door open, so instead of being locked out the
device is allowed straight back in and the numbers get re-synced on the way. That's
why it helps, it's letting the thing recover itself instead of you having to go and
re-pair it by hand.

Thing is it doesn't fix the actual fault, it just stops it getting stuck. The device
is still losing its counter on every power cut, so it carries on dropping and
rejoining, dropping and rejoining. For some people that settles down enough to feel
ok, for others all that constant rejoining seems to make the counter worse and it
starts dropping again after a day or two. And you're leaving the network a bit more
open than it should be the whole time it's on, so it's a trade-off rather than a fix.

I’m no expert on Zigbee, so take this for what it is — this is the workaround ChatGPT helped me work through based on the behaviour/logs and the discussion in this thread.

I’ve now had no issues for around 18 hours, which is much better than before. Previously the ZBMINIL2s would reconnect after resetting/rejoining, work for a couple of hours, and then drop offline again.

My setup is Home Assistant Connect ZBT-2 + ZHA + SONOFF ZBMINIL2 on firmware 1.0.14 / 0x0000100E.

I added the following to my main configuration.yaml:

zha:
  zigpy_config:
    ezsp_policies:
      TRUST_CENTER_POLICY: 0x0002

I then went to Settings → Developer Tools/Tools → YAML, checked the configuration, and restarted Home Assistant.

My ZBT-2 diagnostics had been showing NWK_FRAME_COUNTER_FAILURE events while the APS frame-counter/decryption failure counters stayed at 0, so the theory was that allowing unsecured rejoins might let the ZBMINIL2 recover instead of getting stranded offline.

Since enabling TRUST_CENTER_POLICY: 0x0002, the devices have remained connected / recovered without me repeatedly removing and re-pairing them.

From what I understand, this does not disable Zigbee encryption. It allows already-known devices to perform an unsecured rejoin, which seems to help with this particular failure mode.

I did also update Home Assistant to the latest available version at the same time, so I can’t completely rule that out as a factor. However, as others in this thread have already said, updating HA alone has not fixed the issue for them.

So for me at least, this looks like a working workaround so far — although presumably the underlying ZBMINIL2 power-loss/rejoin problem still needs a proper fix.

Worth a go?

Just a word of caution about leaving unsecured rejoins permanently enabled: this setting applies to the entire Zigbee network, not only to the affected ZBMINIL2 devices. A malicious device located within Zigbee radio range could potentially attempt to access the network through an unsecured rejoin. The attacker would not necessarily need to enter the house, only to be close enough to receive the Zigbee signal.

It may therefore work as a temporary workaround by allowing the ZBMINIL2 to reconnect automatically, but it does not prevent the module from dropping off again and it reduces the security of the whole network.

Your idea of allowing unsecured rejoins only for specific, previously registered IEEE addresses would seem much safer, if ZHA can support it. Until a maintainer confirms this, I would personally be cautious about leaving unsecured rejoins enabled permanently.

Hello, your question is not stupid at all.

Zigbee2MQTT might handle some rejoin situations differently from ZHA, so it is possible that the behaviour could be different. However, there is currently no confirmation that migrating to Zigbee2MQTT permanently fixes this specific ZBMINIL2 problem.

The suspected issue appears to involve the ZBMINIL2 firmware and its rejoin behaviour. Changing from ZHA to Zigbee2MQTT would not change the firmware installed on the module. Similar SONOFF reconnection problems have also previously been reported with Zigbee2MQTT and Silicon Labs/Ember coordinators.

I would therefore strongly advise against deleting your complete ZHA installation just to test this. You would probably have to pair all your Zigbee devices again, and there is no guarantee that the ZBMINIL2 modules would remain connected.

If someone wants to test Zigbee2MQTT, the safer approach would be to use a separate coordinator and move only one affected ZBMINIL2 temporarily, while keeping the existing ZHA network intact.

For now, I think it is better to wait for feedback from the ZHA maintainers and SONOFF rather than rebuilding the entire Zigbee network without knowing whether it will solve the problem.

@ajfhodgson On the per-IEEE idea: not with the policy as it stands, but there may be a mechanism that does exactly what you are asking for. I went through the bellows source and the Silicon Labs SDK, and I would like a maintainer to confirm or kill it.

**What is in place today**

`TRUST_CENTER_POLICY` is a single network-wide bitmask on the coordinator: `ALLOW_JOINS` (0x0001), `ALLOW_UNSECURED_REJOINS` (0x0002), `SEND_KEY_IN_CLEAR` (0x0004), `IGNORE_UNSECURED_REJOINS` (0x0008), `JOINS_USE_INSTALL_CODE_KEY` (0x0010), `DEFER_JOINS` (0x0020), in `bellows/types/named.py`. None of them takes a device address.

The decision is also taken on the NCP, not on the host. `trustCenterJoinHandler` is a notification about a decision that has already been made, and `_handle_tc_join_handler` in `bellows/zigbee/application.py` returns early when it is `DENY_JOIN`. By the time the host sees the IEEE, the answer has gone out.

Opening the network for joining is the same knob set temporarily. `pre_permit` in `bellows/ezsp/v8/__init__.py` sets `ALLOW_JOINS|ALLOW_UNSECURED_REJOINS`, sleeps for the permit duration, then restores the configured `tc_policy`. That is why opening the network is what brings the module back: it grants exactly the unsecured rejoin the device keeps asking for.

**What might give a per-device gate**

The Delayed Join component. The policy gets `DEFER_JOINS` on top, plus `SL_ZIGBEE_EZSP_VALUE_DELAYED_JOIN_ACTIVATION` (0x45) set to 1, and the NCP then holds the network key back instead of sending it (`protocol/zigbee/app/util/ezsp/ezsp-enum.h` and `app/framework/plugin/delayed-join/delayed-join.c` in simplicity_sdk).

The host then releases the key to one specific device with `unicastCurrentNetworkKey`, EZSP frame 0x0050, which takes `targetShort`, `targetLong` (the EUI64) and `parentShortId` (`protocol/zigbee/stack/include/trust-center.h`). No call, no key. That is a per-IEEE gate, and bellows already carries the frame in every version from EZSP v7 (`bellows/ezsp/v7/commands.py`).

**Two things I cannot establish from the sources.** @puddly, these are really questions for you, or for someone who knows what goes into the NCP firmware builds:

1. Does Delayed Join apply to unsecured rejoins, or only to fresh joins? Every description I can find says "new joining device", and the stack code that decides is in the binary libraries.
2. Is the component compiled into the firmware on ZBT-1 / ZBT-2, so that 0x45 can be set at all? I tried to read 0x45 on my own ZBT-2, but zha-toolkit's `ezsp_get_value` calls `app._ezsp.types`, which no longer exists in bellows 1.x, so I could not check.

If both answers are yes, the gate already exists at the protocol level and it becomes a question of wiring it up. If either is no, then unsecured rejoins are all or nothing, which is worth knowing before people leave them enabled.

I am reading the dev branch of bellows and the public simplicity_sdk, and I am not a maintainer, so please correct anything above.

Small follow-up on my question 2 above.

I can read the value now. `EZSP_VALUE_DELAYED_JOIN_ACTIVATION` (0x45) on my ZBT-2 returns status SUCCESS with the value `0x00`.

The value itself is what you would expect, nobody has turned the feature on. The part I find interesting is that it returned SUCCESS rather than an invalid-id error, which suggests the Delayed Join component is in the firmware build and simply not activated. A code-level finding relevant to this report: the ZBMINIL2 sends Keep-Alive (`0x0025`) Read Attributes requests, although its advertised output clusters omit `0x0025`. Zigpy's endpoint/cluster matching can discard such a request before the coordinator's Keep-Alive attribute handler sees it. An isolated replay against zigpy 2.2.0 produces no response with the original descriptor and a matching response when the missing client cluster is added. This is addressed by the existing proposals [zigpy/zigpy#1888](https://github.com/zigpy/zigpy/pull/1888) and [zha-device-handlers#5349](https://github.com/zigpy/zha-device-handlers/pull/5349).

I also found that zigpy 2.2.0 does not request APS encryption for Keep-Alive responses. [ZCL revision 8 §3.18.4](https://zigbeealliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/07-5123-08-Zigbee-Cluster-Library.pdf) requires an APS-encrypted Read Attributes response for this liveness check. I left the specific code observation on [zigpy/zigpy#1888](https://github.com/zigpy/zigpy/pull/1888#issuecomment-5817075719).

These are reproducible host-side interoperability defects. Their contribution to each reported rejoin/leave episode still requires longer field validation.

MCP Server: requests with method "server/discover" log a 90-line root WARNING and return -32602

### The problem

The Model Context Protocol Server integration does not implement `server/discover`, which the MCP specification 2026-07-28 requires ("Servers MUST implement it"). MCP clients that follow that revision (for example recent Claude Code CLI releases) send `server/discover` first and then fall back to the `initialize` handshake, so tools keep working — but every connection writes a ~90-line pydantic validation dump to the log:

- the message is logged on the root logger (`[root]`), so it cannot be silenced per integration and shows up in log-based monitoring as an error flood;
- the reply is JSON-RPC error -32602 (Invalid params) instead of -32601 (Method not found), for any unknown method, not only `server/discover`.

The behaviour comes from the MCP Python SDK 1.x session handling, which the integration pins (`mcp==1.26.0` in 2026.9, `mcp==1.28.1` on dev). Ness Alarm: hard-coded 5 s polling floods panel, arm/disarm commands lost

### The problem

### The problem
Since the Ness Alarm integration was moved to the UI, `DEFAULT_SCAN_INTERVAL` in `const.py` is hard-coded to 5 seconds, and there is no longer any option to change it (the old YAML `scan_interval` is gone).

Each cycle sends four status requests (S00, S20, S14, S18). The D8x/D16x panel answers roughly one request every 1.6 seconds, so requests pile up faster than they are answered. After a few minutes, arm and disarm commands are written to the interface but never acted on by the panel. Reloading the integration clears the backlog temporarily, then the problem returns.

### Fix confirmed
A custom copy of the integration with `DEFAULT_SCAN_INTERVAL = timedelta(seconds=60)` fixes it. Arm and disarm are confirmed by the panel within 0.3 seconds, tested repeatedly over 45+ minutes, and zones still update instantly via panel events.

Suggest restoring the scan interval as a configurable option, or defaulting to 60 seconds.

### Environment
- Home Assistant Core 2026.9.3 (HAOS, HA Green)
- Ness D16x, firmware 7.8
- IP232 interface, shared with a Ness Z-Wave gateway on the same interface
- Likely the same root cause as #168668

2026.9.3

Meh. Any chance the SmartHome integration could get a proper fix that keeps track of those repeaters as "configured, but useless" instead of discarding them after setup? Having ignored devices in my setup kinda triggers my OCD 🥴 > Any chance the SmartHome integration could get a proper fix that keeps track of those repeaters as "configured, but useless" instead of discarding them after setup? I'm not aware of any, and further as I don't own such a repeater, I can't investigate it. Would be great if you could provide the SSDP information of the repater - you'll find them in Home Assistant under **Settings > System > Network > SSDP Browser** search for `fbox`, now open each entry for that repeater (_check the IP in the section title_), use the "copy to clipboard" on the bottom right and paste the content "as-is" here i a comment example: Fritz!Repeater 1200AX shows 4 SSDP entries pointing to the same fboxdesc.xml: STs are - upnp:rootdevice - urn:schemas-any-com:service:fritzbox:1 - urn:schemas-upnp-org:device:fritzbox:1 - uuid:123402409-bccb-40e7-8e6c-60B58D8855B6 Full dump of the _upnp:rootdevice_ entry: ```json { "name": "repeaterschlafzimmer", "ssdp_usn": "uuid:123402409-bccb-40e7-8e6c-249900B6C043::upnp:rootdevice", "ssdp_st": "upnp:rootdevice", "upnp": { "deviceType": "urn:schemas-upnp-org:device:fritzbox:1", "friendlyName": "repeaterschlafzimmer", "manufacturer": "FRITZ! The 1610 (falsely?) also advertises both a igddesc.xml and a igd2desc.xml This dump is almost the same as for my FRITZ!Box (_besides the uuid, ip, model name_) ... none of the, considered to be stable, fields and values can be used to clearly identify this device a a pure repeater without any smart home features - even the content of `fboxdesc.xml` and `fboxSCPD.xml` (_checked on my FRITZ!Box_) doesn't allow a stable and reproducible way to distinguish between a full-featured FRITZ!Box and a repeater. Also the history of FRITZ! (_former AVM_) taught us, that considering the model name as stable for the life-time of a device is a wrong assumption. So, ignoring the devices is the _best_ solution. Hi @DukeSniper sorry for long delay, but I've got a new idea how to hopefully identify a non-smarthome-device, but to double-check it before I'm going to implement it, could you please provide the response of `http://IPADDRESS:49000/tr64desc.xml` (_replace `IPADDRESS` with the proper ip-address of your repeaters and fritzbox_) for your repeaters and fritzbox routers? query:
UniFi Protect vehicle event drops license plates when a crossing line overlaps the zone detection

### The problem

`event.<camera>_vehicle` (`ProtectDeviceVehicleEventEntity`) loses the license plate for about half of the vehicles that cross a Protect crossing line. It either fires without `license_plate` or doesn't fire at all. Protect has the plate for every one of them: it shows in the Protect console and in the stored event's `metadata.detectedThumbnails[].group.matchedName`.

Setup: a G6 Bullet with vehicle and license plate detection, one smart detection zone and one crossing line (arrival direction). Over 10 days there were 34 vehicle line crossings, and Protect stored a plate for all 34. The vehicle entity delivered the plate for 18, fired without a plate for 9, and did not fire for 7. I reproduced it with a controlled test: drive out, drive back in across the line, and the entity did not fire.

**Cause.** When a vehicle crosses the line, Protect runs two overlapping events for it: a `smartDetectZone` event (start T) and a `smartDetectLine` event (start T+3…40 s). Both have `smartDetectTypes: [licensePlate, vehicle]` and the same plate thumbnail. Example (local time):

| event | start | end | plate thumbnail |
|---|---|---|---|
| smartDetectZone | 09:19:54.270 | 09:20:20.903 | `7ABC123`, clockBestWall 09:20:09.983 |
| smartDetectLine | 09:20:05.332 | 09:20:20.903 | `7ABC123`, clockBestWall 09:20:09.983 |

The vehicle entity reads `camera.last_smart_detect_event` (`ufp_event_obj="last_smart_detect_event"`) every time the camera is signaled, and only acts when `event.type is EventType.SMART_DETECT`. `data.py` signals the camera for every event message; it does not pass along which event changed. In uiprotect, `_process_smart_detect_event` moves the singular `last_smart_detect_event_id` to the newest active event, so the line event takes it at T+n. From then on, updates to the zone event, including the one that carries the plate, are read against the line event and skipped.

Whether the plate gets through depends on how the two events end:

| end order | plate delivered |
|---|---|
| zone event ends after the line event | 13 / 13 |
| both end in the same millisecond | 4 / 18 |
| zone event ends first | 1 / 2 |

If the line event ends while the zone event is still active, uiprotect hands the singular pointer back to the zone event, and the entity reads the final plate. When both end together, it depends on which end frame is processed first.

**Live confirmation.** A websocket trace (a second subscriber on the same `ProtectApiClient`) during the test arrival. Times are UTC; `slot` is the type of the camera's `last_smart_detect_event` after each update:

| time | update | slot |
|---|---|---|
| 17:58:17.955 | zone event opens | zone |
| 17:58:22.496 | line event opens | **line** |
| 17:58:33.605 | zone event `end` | line (update skipped) |
| 17:58:33.751 | line event `end` | line |
| 17:58:33.862 | zone event `metadata` with the vehicle thumbnail | line (skipped) |

`event.<camera>_vehicle` never fired for this vehicle. Its last state change was a different car 27 s earlier.

**Suggested fix.** Process the event from the websocket message rather than the camera's singular pointer (for example, pass the changed event through, or track the vehicle event by id via `camera.get_last_smart_detect_event(SmartDetectObjectType.VEHICLE)`). Also treat `smartDetectLine` vehicle events as vehicle detections. The binary sensors were fixed for the same zone/line overlap in uilibs/uiprotect#778 and #167108.

### What version of Home Assistant Core has the issue?

core-2026.9.3 (the vehicle entity code is unchanged in 2026.9.4 and `dev`)

### What was the last working version of Home Assistant Core?

_No response_

### What type of installation are you running?

Home Assistant OS

### Integration causing the issue

UniFi Protect

### Link to integration documentation on our website

https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/unifiprotect/

### Diagnostics information

UniFi Protect 7.2.105 on a UDM Pro Max; uiprotect 16.6.1. Camera: G6 Bullet.

### Example YAML snippet

_No response_

### Anything in the logs that might be useful for us?

```txt
DEBUG uiprotect.api: emitting message: update:event:<zone id>:['camera_id', 'device_id', 'end', 'id']
DEBUG uiprotect.api: emitting message: update:event:<line id>:['camera_id', 'device_id', 'end', 'id']
DEBUG uiprotect.api: emitting message: update:event:<zone id>:['metadata']
DEBUG uiprotect.api: emitting message: update:event:<line id>:['metadata']
```

No errors or warnings. The zone event's final `metadata` update arrives while the camera's pointer is on the line event.

### Additional information

Where the plate appears, live vs. stored:

- In live websocket updates the vehicle thumbnail had `group: null`, with the plate in both `name` and `attributes.matchedName`, plus OCR alternatives in `attributes.topKCandidate` / `namesTopK`.
- In the stored event (`GET /api/events`), the same thumbnail has `group.matchedName` = the plate, and `group.name` / `name` = the vehicle's saved label in Protect (for example "My Car").

`_build_event_data` reads `group.matched_name` and falls back to `name`, which covers the live case. If a frame ever arrives with a group attached, though, `name` is the saved label rather than the plate, so reading `attributes.matchedName` would be more robust.

Related: uilibs/uiprotect#778, home-assistant/core#167108, #168126, #179508, #157203.

query:
Tile: last_timestamp and last_lost_timestamp are shifted by the local UTC offset

### The problem

The Tile device tracker's `last_timestamp` and `last_lost_timestamp` attributes are shifted by the local UTC offset. With the time zone set to America/Chicago, a location fix at 16:31:20 UTC shows as `last_timestamp: 2026-09-27T21:31:20.996000+00:00` (5 hours late in CDT, 6 in CST). `last_lost_timestamp` shows `1970-01-01T05:59:59.999000+00:00`: one millisecond before the epoch, shifted by the CST offset.

pytile 2024.12.0 returns both as naive datetimes holding UTC (`pytile/tile.py`, `_save_timestamps`):

```python
self._last_timestamp = datetime.fromtimestamp(
    last_state["timestamp"] / 1000, tz=timezone.utc
).replace(tzinfo=None)
```

`homeassistant/components/tile/device_tracker.py` passes them to `as_utc`, which reads a naive datetime as the configured time zone:

```python
self._attr_extra_state_attributes[timestamp_attr[0]] = as_utc(
    timestamp_attr[1]
)
```

Only installs running in UTC get correct values. West of UTC the fix time lands in the future; east of UTC it lands in the past. West of UTC, a check that the fix is no older than 15 minutes fails for every current fix.

Suggested fix: `timestamp_attr[1].replace(tzinfo=dt_util.UTC)` in place of `as_utc(timestamp_attr[1])`.

### What version of Home Assistant Core has the issue?

core-2026.9.3; the same code and pytile pin are on `dev` as of 2026-09-27

### What was the last working version of Home Assistant Core?

_No response_

### What type of installation are you running?

Home Assistant OS

### Integration causing the issue

Tile

### Link to integration documentation on our website

https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/tile

### Diagnostics information

_No response_

### Example YAML snippet

```yaml
# True west of UTC for a recent fix: the reported fix time is in the future.
{{ as_timestamp(state_attr('device_tracker.my_tile', 'last_timestamp')) > as_timestamp(now()) }}
```

### Anything in the logs that might be useful for us?

_No response_

### Additional information

Host, Supervisor and Home Assistant time zones are all America/Chicago. Seen on two Tiles on one account.

query:
Calendar: event listeners accumulate and every refresh runs one uncached async_get_events per listener on the event loop

### The problem

### The problem

Calendar entities keep one event listener per subscribing frontend card. On every coordinator refresh, `async_update_event_listeners()` iterates over all registered listeners and performs a **separate, uncached** `async_get_events()` expansion for each one, on the event loop.

The listener list grows over the lifetime of the instance and is apparently not fully released when websocket clients disconnect uncleanly. The result is a slow-motion failure: the event loop stalls once per refresh interval, the stall grows linearly with uptime, and eventually the Supervisor watchdog misses two consecutive API responses and force-restarts Home Assistant. After the restart the cycle starts over.

This is not a misconfiguration — the entire installation has only four calendar cards, each showing the same two entities (one Google calendar and one non-Google calendar). Four cards cannot legitimately produce 225 live listeners on one entity.

### Measurements

**1. The stall is periodic and grows linearly with uptime.**

Measured without any instrumentation, as gaps in the recorder history of a KNX electricity meter that sends a new value every 5 seconds. Any gap longer than 20 s is a stalled event loop. The window below is one full cycle between two watchdog-forced restarts (18.5 hours):

| Hour since restart | Stalls in that hour | Longest stall |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 4 | 23 s |
| 4 | 4 | 37 s |
| 6 | 4 | 41 s |
| 8 | 4 | 52 s |
| 10 | 4 | 58 s |
| 12 | 4 | 61 s |
| 14 | 4 | 68 s |
| 16 | 4 | 80 s |
| 18 | 8 | 143 s -> forced restart |

Exactly **four stalls per hour**, matching the 15-minute Google Calendar coordinator interval, and growth of roughly **4 s per hour** (~1 s per cycle).

**2. The CPU profile shows where the time goes.**

`profiler.start` over 1500 s, taken 3.3 h after a restart:

| Function | Calls | Cumulative |
|---|---|---|
| `calendar/__init__.py:713 async_update_event_listeners` | 2 | 28.71 s |
| `google/calendar.py:427 async_get_events` | 450 | 28.85 s |
| `ical/iter.py:272 __next__` | 71,447 | 49.87 s |
| `ical/iter.py:357 overlapping` | 4,321 | 27.89 s |
| `ical/timespan.py:96 __lt__` | 716,805 | 9.55 s |

Two refresh cycles, 450 expansions — **225 listeners on a single calendar entity**, against four calendar cards in the whole installation. Two of those cards run permanently on wall-mounted displays, one of which reconnects frequently; the listener count tracks uptime, not the number of cards.

**3. The cost per expansion does not depend on the requested window.**

Measured on a calendar with 251 events, requesting one-day windows at various points between 2015 and 2026: consistently 0.86–1.26 s, **including for windows containing no events at all**. Every call rebuilds the full timeline from all events. A second calendar with 526 events costs 0.08 s per call, so the dominant factor is recurrence-rule expansion, not event count.

**4. Mitigation attempt confirms the mechanism.**

Removing the two most expensive calendars from the cards dropped the per-call cost from 1.18 s to 0.064 s. Stall growth fell from 7.8 s to ~1 s per cycle — an 8x improvement — but the **listener count returned to the same level** (228 before, 225 after), and forced restarts resumed two days later. Reducing per-call cost only postpones the failure; it does not address the accumulation.

### Impact

Before the mitigation: 49–61 watchdog misses and 4–5 forced restarts per day. After: 16–20 misses and 1 forced restart per day, roughly every 18.5 hours. During each stall the instance is fully unresponsive — the UI, the API, the local MQTT broker ("No ACK from MQTT server in 10 seconds") and all cloud connections time out simultaneously. Nothing is logged during the stall itself, which makes this hard to diagnose from logs alone: the visible errors are all downstream timeouts that appear *after* the loop resumes.

### Expected behavior

A calendar refresh should cost about one event expansion per entity, not one per subscriber, and the listener list should not grow without bound.

### Suggested directions

1. **Deduplicate** listeners with identical `(start_date, end_date)` ranges within one refresh and share the result — this alone would collapse 225
   identical expansions into one.
2. **Cache** the expansion per entity per refresh cycle.
3. **Verify listener cleanup** on websocket disconnect. 225 listeners for four cards suggests subscriptions survive dropped connections. One display in this installation reconnects frequently (it logs "Client unable to keep up with pending messages. Reached 4096 pending"), which matches the observed accumulation rate.
4. Consider moving the expansion off the event loop, or bounding it.

### Environment

- Home Assistant Core 2026.9.1, Supervisor 2026.09.0, HA OS 18.2
- Home Assistant Green, Python 3.14
- Integration: `google` (Google Calendar), 8 calendar entities total, 6 of them Google
- 4 calendar cards across 7 dashboards; two of the dashboards run permanently on wall-mounted displays

### Relevant code

`homeassistant/components/calendar/__init__.py`:

    for start_date, end_date, listener in self._event_listeners:
        self.async_update_single_event_listener(start_date, end_date, listener)

No caching and no deduplication: identical time ranges across different
listeners each trigger a separate fetch.

query:
Alexa: AdjustRangeValue is rejected when a cover is fully closed (current_position == 0)

### The problem

`async_api_adjust_range` treats a cover position of `0` as "position unknown"
and aborts, because the guard is a truthiness check rather than a `None` check:

```python
# homeassistant/components/alexa/handlers.py (dev, lines 1618-1626)
# Cover Position
if instance == f"{COVER_DOMAIN}.{cover.ATTR_POSITION}":
    range_delta = int(range_delta * 20) if range_delta_default else int(range_delta)
    service = SERVICE_SET_COVER_POSITION
    if not (
        current := entity.attributes.get(CoverEntityStateAttribute.CURRENT_POSITION)
    ):
        msg = f"Unable to determine {entity.entity_id} current position"
        raise AlexaInvalidValueError(msg)
```

`0` is falsy, so a cover that is fully closed — a perfectly known position, and
arguably the most common starting point for a relative adjustment — makes Home
Assistant answer with `Alexa.ErrorResponse` / `INVALID_VALUE`. Alexa renders
that to the user as a refusal ("that's not supported"), which reads like a
missing capability rather than a bug.

The same defect is in the tilt branch a few lines below (dev, lines 1639-1642):

```python
current = entity.attributes.get(cover.ATTR_TILT_POSITION)
if not current:
    msg = f"Unable to determine {entity.entity_id} current tilt position"
    raise AlexaInvalidValueError(msg)
```

Consequence for users: "Alexa, open the blinds by 10%" works from any position
except fully closed. Opening the cover by any amount, by any other means, makes
the identical utterance work. `SetRangeValue` ("set the opening to 10%") is
unaffected — it never reads the current position.

### History

The error message itself was reported in #121741 and closed by #121798 in July
2024, but that PR only corrected the attribute name (`position` →
`current_position`). The truthiness check predates it and was left untouched;
it is still on `dev` today.

### Suggested fix

```python
if (
    current := entity.attributes.get(CoverEntityStateAttribute.CURRENT_POSITION)
) is None:
```

and, for tilt:

```python
current = entity.attributes.get(cover.ATTR_TILT_POSITION)
if current is None:
```

The arithmetic right below already clamps with `min(100, max(0, range_delta + current))`,
and both `position == 0` and `position == 100` are already special-cased to
`close_cover` / `open_cover`, so no other change is needed.

The existing tests pass a non-zero position (`test_cover_position_range` uses
`current_position: 30`), which is why this is not caught. A parametrisation
with `0` would cover it.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Expose a cover that supports `SET_POSITION` to a self-hosted Alexa Smart
   Home skill. It is discovered with `Alexa.RangeController`,
   `instance: cover.position`, `supportedRange` 0-100, `precision` 1, plus the
   usual open/close/raise/lower semantics.
2. Close the cover fully, so `current_position == 0`.
3. Say a relative adjustment, e.g. "Alexa, open <cover> by 10%".
   → Alexa refuses; Home Assistant returned `INVALID_VALUE`.
4. Open the cover slightly by any other means, so `current_position > 0`.
5. Say the identical phrase. → Works.

### What version of Home Assistant Core has the issue?

2026.8.2 (also present on `dev` at the time of writing)

### What was the last working version of Home Assistant Core?

Unknown — the truthiness check predates #121798 (July 2024) and is unchanged.

### What type of installation are you running?

Home Assistant Container

### Integration causing the issue

alexa

### Link to integration documentation on our website

https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/alexa.smart_home/

### Diagnostics information

_No response_

### Example YAML snippet

```yaml
alexa:
  smart_home:
    locale: it-IT
    filter:
      include_entities:
        - cover.tapparella_soggiorno   # MQTT cover, supported_features 15
```

```txt

```

### Additional information

Reproduced deterministically on a Zigbee shutter exposed through MQTT
(`supported_features: 15` — open/close/set_position/stop), locale `it-IT`.
Closed: refused every time. Open by any amount: works every time.

query:
MQTT: `KeyError` in `get_subscription_id` after quick unsubscribe/resubscribe of a wildcard topic breaks all later (re)subscriptions until restart

### The problem

## The problem

If an integration unsubscribes a wildcard topic and subscribes to the same topic again while the UNSUBSCRIBE is still waiting for its UNSUBACK, the MQTT client drops the topic's subscription identifier while the new subscription still needs it. The next subscribe pass then fails with `KeyError` in `SubscriptionID.get_subscription_id()`.

The error does not stay with that one topic:

- The failed topic never gets subscribed, so its callbacks get no messages.
- The exception aborts the whole `_async_perform_subscriptions` pass, so other pending subscriptions in the same pass are skipped too.
- The topic stays in `_wildcard_subscriptions` without a registered id. After every broker reconnect, the resubscribe pass hits the same `KeyError` again, and subscriptions for **every** MQTT integration are lost.

Only restarting HA recovers.

Real-world impact here: after one reload of the `ramses_cc` config entry followed by a Mosquitto add-on restart, the EMS-ESP boiler sensors (a separate MQTT integration) stopped updating. `sensor.boiler_curflowtemp` normally updates every 10–40 s. It got one value on reconnect (18:34:11) and then nothing until I restarted HA at 18:39.

## What version of Home Assistant Core has the issue?

core-2026.9.3

## What was the last working version of Home Assistant Core?

Not verified. Probably any version before MQTT v5 subscription identifiers were added in #169604 (2026.6).

## What type of installation are you running?

Home Assistant OS (18.2, Supervisor 2026.09.2), Mosquitto add-on, MQTT protocol 5.

## Integration causing the issue

MQTT

## Link to integration documentation on our website

https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/mqtt/

## Diagnostics information

Attached: `mqtt_diag_attach.json` (MQTT config entry, taken while stuck; version and broker config only, credentials already redacted by HA).

## Example YAML snippet

N/A. Triggered by a custom integration (`ramses_cc`) that subscribes wildcard topics through `mqtt.async_subscribe`: `RAMSES/GATEWAY/+/rx`, `RAMSES/GATEWAY/+/cmd/result`, `RAMSES/GATEWAY/+`. On reload it unsubscribes them all and subscribes again about 130 ms later.

## Anything in the logs that might be useful for us?

```

2026-09-26 18:28:58.974 DEBUG [custom_components.ramses_cc.mqtt_pool_bridge] MqttPoolBridge: Subscribing to wildcard RX RAMSES/GATEWAY/+/rx
2026-09-26 18:28:58.974 DEBUG [custom_components.ramses_cc.mqtt_pool_bridge] MqttPoolBridge: Subscribing to wildcard CMD RAMSES/GATEWAY/+/cmd/result
2026-09-26 18:28:58.974 DEBUG [custom_components.ramses_cc.mqtt_pool_bridge] MqttPoolBridge: Subscribing to wildcard status RAMSES/GATEWAY/+
2026-09-26 18:28:59.074 ERROR (MainThread) [homeassistant] Error doing job: Task exception was never retrieved (task: None)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/usr/src/homeassistant/homeassistant/components/mqtt/util.py", line 79, in _async_job
    await self._callback()
  File "/usr/src/homeassistant/homeassistant/components/mqtt/client.py", line 1102, in _async_perform_subscriptions
    self._mqtt_data.subscription_id_generator.get_subscription_id(topic)
  File "/usr/src/homeassistant/homeassistant/components/mqtt/models.py", line 87, in get_subscription_id
    return self._registered_subscriptions[topic]
KeyError: 'RAMSES/GATEWAY/+/rx'

# Mosquitto add-on restarted to test recovery:
2026-09-26 18:34:01.553 WARNING [homeassistant.components.mqtt.client] Error returned from MQTT server: The connection was lost.
2026-09-26 18:34:11.940 ERROR (MainThread) [homeassistant] Error doing job: Task exception was never retrieved (task: None)
  ... same traceback ...
KeyError: 'RAMSES/GATEWAY/+/rx'
```

On an earlier day (2026-09-24), the same sequence failed on `KeyError: 'RAMSES/GATEWAY/+/cmd/result'`. The failing topic is whichever one gets hit first.

Trimmed log attached: `ha_mqtt_keyerror_attach.log`.

## Additional information

### Likely cause (code refs from 2026.9.3)

1. `_async_perform_unsubscribes()` (client.py ~1140) copies `_pending_unsubscribes` into `topics`, clears the set, sends UNSUBSCRIBE and **awaits** `_async_wait_for_mid_or_raise(mid, result)`. Only after that does it call `subscription_id_generator.release(topic)` for every topic in `topics`.
2. During that await, the integration calls `async_subscribe()` on the same wildcard topic. `get_or_generate(topic)` returns the id that is still registered. `_async_queue_subscriptions()` (client.py ~958) removes the topic from `_pending_unsubscribes`, but that set was already copied and cleared in step 1, so it has no effect.
3. The await finishes, and `release(topic)` pops the registration, even though the topic now has an active subscription again (tracked in `_wildcard_subscriptions`, queued in `_pending_subscriptions`).
4. The debounced `_async_perform_subscriptions()` calls `get_subscription_id(topic)` (client.py 1102), which does a plain dict lookup → `KeyError`. The pass aborts.
5. On reconnect, `_async_queue_resubscribe()` requeues every active subscription, including this one, which still has no registered id, so every later resubscribe pass fails at the same point.

### Possible fix

Either or both:

- In `_async_perform_unsubscribes()`, skip `release(topic)` for topics that were subscribed again while waiting for the UNSUBACK (e.g. `topic in self._pending_subscriptions` or the topic still has an active subscription).
- In `_async_perform_subscriptions()`, use `get_or_generate(topic)` instead of `get_subscription_id(topic)`, so a missing id can't abort the whole pass.

### Reproduce

1. MQTT v5 broker (the Mosquitto add-on is fine).
2. From an integration: `unsub = await mqtt.async_subscribe(hass, "test/+/rx", cb)`, then `unsub()`, then about 50–150 ms later (after the unsubscribe debounce fires, before the UNSUBACK arrives) `await mqtt.async_subscribe(hass, "test/+/rx", cb)` again.

ViCare: blocking call to putrequest causes full event loop freeze / Supervisor watchdog restart loop after 2026.9.0

### The problem

### The problem

After manually updating Home Assistant Core to 2026.9.0, our ViCare-based
heat pump setup (Viessmann Vitocal, accessed via the official `vicare`
integration) started causing repeated full Home Assistant Core freezes,
approximately every 68–71 minutes, forcing the Supervisor watchdog to
kill and restart Home Assistant Core.

Home Assistant's own blocking-call detector logs the following on
almost every polling attempt (via `homeassistant.update_entity`):

Caught blocking call to putrequest with args
(<HTTPSConnection(host='api.viessmann-climatesolutions.com', port=443)>,
'GET', '/iot/v2/features/installations/.../gateways/.../devices/0/features/')
inside the event loop by integration 'vicare' at
homeassistant/components/vicare/api.py, line 26:
return super().request(method, url, **kwargs).
(offender: urllib3/connection.py, line 406: return super().putrequest())

For plain sensor entities, this is caught and only aborts the calling
automation (logged as an ERROR, automation fails, but Core keeps running).

For `climate` and `fan` platform entities specifically, the same
blocking call appears to actually freeze the event loop long enough
that Supervisor's watchdog stops receiving API responses and force-
restarts Home Assistant Core entirely — this happened like clockwork
roughly every 70 minutes, all night and into the next day, for about
24 hours straight.

### Timeline / reproduction

- Manually updated Core to 2026.9.0 on 2026-09-04 at approx. 14:15 local time.
- First forced Core restart (via Supervisor watchdog) occurred at 14:18:38,
  and continued every ~68–71 minutes without interruption (with one
  short-interval exception caused by a manual power cycle during
  unrelated troubleshooting) until the ViCare integration was fully
  disabled.
- Removing the `climate` and `fan` entities from our `homeassistant.update_entity`
  polling automations reduced but did not eliminate the crash loop
  (still crashed again ~70 minutes later, triggered via a plain sensor
  entity's cache refresh instead).
- As a controlled test, we fully disabled the ViCare config entry
  (Settings > Devices & Services > Viessmann ViCare > Disable) at 11:07.
  The Supervisor watchdog restart loop stopped immediately and has not
  recurred for 90+ consecutive minutes since (longer than any single
  crash-free interval observed since the 2026.9.0 update), while every
  comparable interval before disabling contained at least one forced
  restart.
- Re-enabling is expected to reproduce the issue (not yet tested, to
  avoid further instability).

### Suspected cause

This is a related but distinct occurrence of the same underlying issue
as #125443 ("Blocking call in event loop in ViCare integration",
closed Dec 2024). That issue was fixed narrowly for the `getSerial()`
call during entity setup (see PR #125495), fixing the specific call
site at `vicare/entity.py` line 39.

However, the same root cause — PyViCare's `fetch_all_features()` making
a synchronous, blocking HTTP request whenever its internal cache is
stale — is not limited to entity setup. Any entity's property access
(climate, fan, or plain sensors) can trigger this same blocking call
during normal runtime operation, not just at startup.

This appears to have become newly reproducible/more severe after
2026.9.0 (first in 2026.9.0b1), which includes:
"Fix ViCare setup by passing the accessor to fetch_all_features" (#180315)

This change may have altered how/when the cache refresh is triggered,
resurfacing the same class of bug through a different code path than
the one fixed in #125495.

For plain sensor entities, Home Assistant's blocking-call detector
cleanly raises and aborts only the calling automation/update — Core
keeps running. For `climate` and `fan` entities specifically, the same
blocking call appears to actually freeze the event loop long enough
to trip the Supervisor watchdog, causing a full Core restart roughly
every 68-71 minutes in our case.

Still reproducible on HA Core 2026.9.3 with a Miele freezer (`FREEZER`, type 20), pymiele 0.6.2.

Two things I can contribute: a reproducible measurement, and the finding that the API side is not broken at all.

### The appliance status tracks correctly — the switch never follows

I toggled SuperFrost through a template switch calling `switch.turn_on` / `switch.turn_off` on the Miele entity, and recorded both entities:

| Time | `sensor.gefrierschrank` (state_status) | `switch.gefrierschrank_superfrost` |
|------|----------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| 14:17:44 | `superfreezing` | `off` |
| 14:20:31 | `in_use` | `off` |
| 14:21:13 | `superfreezing` | `off` |
| 14:21:41 | `in_use` | `off` |
| 14:22:00 | `superfreezing` | `off` |
| 14:22:11 | `in_use` | `off` |

Three full on/off cycles. SuperFrost really was running each time (confirmed in the Miele iOS app). The status sensor follows the appliance to the second. The switch entity did not change state once, in either direction.

Since `MieleStatusSensor` renders `StateStatus(self.device.state_status).name` and showed `superfreezing`, the coordinator clearly held `state_status == 13` during those windows.

### Which is what makes this odd

`MieleSuperSwitch.is_on` compares exactly that value:

```python
return (
    self.entity_description.value_fn(self.device)   # state_status -> 13
    == self.entity_description.on_value             # StateStatus.superfreezing -> 13
)
```

`MieleEnum` is an `IntEnum` in pymiele 0.6.2, so that comparison should be `True`, and both entities read the same coordinator data. I could not find the defect by reading the source — `switch.py` is byte-identical between 2026.9.3 and `dev`, the switch definition and the `entity_class` selection both look right. So whatever breaks this is not visible in the obvious place, and I would rather report that honestly than guess.

Happy to supply integration diagnostics captured *while SuperFrost is running* if that would help — just say the word.

### STOP_SUPERFREEZE is not broken

This part I am confident about, and it matters for anyone stuck right now.

Calling `switch.turn_off` on the Miele entity **does** stop SuperFrost, reliably, every time (rows 2, 4 and 6 above). The service is not gated on the displayed state — `switch/services.py` registers it straight onto `async_turn_off`:

```python
component.async_register_entity_service(SERVICE_TURN_OFF, None, "async_turn_off")
```

So the call reaches `STOP_SUPERFREEZE` regardless of what the UI shows. Users are stuck only because the toggle reads `off` and therefore sends `turn_on` on the next click. Calling the action directly (Developer Tools → Actions) works around it today.

### Workaround

A template switch restores full control without touching the integration:

```yaml
value_template: >
  {{ states('sensor.gefrierschrank') in ['superfreezing', 'supercooling_superfreezing'] }}
turn_on:
  - action: switch.turn_on
    target:
      entity_id: switch.gefrierschrank_superfrost
turn_off:
  - action: switch.turn_off
    target:
      entity_id: switch.gefrierschrank_superfrost
```

Replace the two entity IDs with your own. The state now follows the appliance, and because the switch actually reads `on` while SuperFrost runs, a click sends `turn_off` instead of `turn_on` again.

http: every unauthenticated request returns 500 instead of 401 when `gethostbyaddr()` on the client IP raises `UnicodeDecodeError`

## Environment

- Home Assistant Core **2026.8.3**, container install (`ghcr.io/home-assistant/home-assistant:stable`), Python **3.14**, aiohttp 3.14.x.
- Reverse-DNS answers on this LAN are produced by the ISP router (an all-in-one gateway that also does DHCP). The router answers PTR queries for its DHCP clients with a **malformed name** (details below).
- No custom components installed; `configuration.yaml` has no `http:` block.

## Description

Requests that fail authentication are supposed to answer `401 Unauthorized`. When the client's
reverse DNS answer is not decodable as UTF-8, the request instead answers **`500 Internal Server
Error`**, and nothing about the failed authentication is logged or counted.

Reproduced for every endpoint that requires auth (`GET /api/`, `GET /api/config`, `GET
/api/states`, with no `Authorization` header, and with an invalid one). Public endpoints are
unaffected: `GET /`, `GET /manifest.json`, `GET /auth/providers` all return 200, and the WebSocket
API authenticates normally. This makes a plain "did my token arrive correctly?" check look like a
server failure.

## Steps to reproduce

1. On a network whose reverse DNS for the client address returns a name containing invalid UTF-8
   (in our case the router answers PTR for `192.168.1.69` with a single 4-byte label
   `40 8a ed be`), request any auth-required endpoint without a token:
   `curl -i http://<ha>:8123/api/`
2. Observe `HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error` with body `500 Internal Server Error / Server got
   itself in trouble`, instead of `401`.

Same network, minimal Python reproduction of the failing lookup (inside the HA container):

```
$ docker exec Home-Assistant-Container python -c "import socket; socket.gethostbyaddr('192.168.1.69')"
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x8a in position 1: invalid start byte
```

## Traceback (from `/config/home-assistant.log`, verbatim)

```
2026-09-21 11:54:39.125 ERROR (MainThread) [aiohttp.server] Error handling request from 192.168.1.69
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/usr/src/homeassistant/homeassistant/components/http/ban.py", line 88, in ban_middleware
    return await handler(request)
  File "/usr/src/homeassistant/homeassistant/components/http/auth.py", line 261, in auth_middleware
    return await handler(request)
  File "/usr/src/homeassistant/homeassistant/components/http/headers.py", line 39, in headers_middleware
    response = await handler(request)
  ...
  File "/usr/src/homeassistant/homeassistant/components/http/request_context.py", line 24, in request_context_middleware
    return await handler(request)
  File "/usr/src/homeassistant/homeassistant/components/http/ban.py", line 90, in ban_middleware
    await process_wrong_login(request)
  File "/usr/src/homeassistant/homeassistant/components/http/ban.py", line 123, in process_wrong_login
    remote_host, _, _ = await hass.async_add_executor_job(
        gethostbyaddr, request.remote
    )
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.14/concurrent/futures/thread.py", line 86, in run
    result = ctx.run(self.task)
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.14/concurrent/futures/thread.py", line 73, in run
    return fn(*args, **kwargs)
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x8a in position 1: invalid start byte
```

## Root cause

`homeassistant/components/http/ban.py::ban_middleware` treats a failed authentication as a wrong
login and calls `process_wrong_login(request)` (line 90). That function resolves the client
hostname for its log message:

```python
async def process_wrong_login(request: Request) -> None:
    hass = request.app[KEY_HASS]
    assert request.remote
    remote_addr = ip_address(request.remote)
    remote_host = request.remote
    with suppress(herror):                     # <-- only herror is tolerated
        remote_host, _, _ = await hass.async_add_executor_job(
            gethostbyaddr, request.remote
        )
```

`socket.gethostbyaddr()` decodes the PTR target as strict UTF-8. A PTR record whose name is not
valid UTF-8 therefore raises `UnicodeDecodeError` (a `ValueError`, not a `herror`), which the
`suppress(herror)` does not cover. Because this happens inside an aiohttp middleware, the intended
`401` never reaches the client: the request ends as a `500`.

Two aggravating consequences, both silent:

1. `process_wrong_login` raises **before** its own `_LOGGER.warning("Login attempt or request with
   invalid authentication from ...")` line and **before** the failed-attempt counter is
   incremented, so:
   - no failed-login warning is ever written,
   - the IP-ban/failed-login counter never advances, i.e. brute-force protection is silently
     disabled for as long as such a PTR answer is in play.
2. Every unauthenticated request writes a full traceback to the log (log noise that looks like an
   internal error rather than a client error).

The malformed answer is real, and it is the router's, not HA's (AdGuard Home's query log records the
raw upstream response for `69.1.168.192.in-addr.arpa` with `"Upstream":"192.168.1.1:53"`; decoding
the logged `Answer` field gives a PTR record whose RDATA is a single label of length 4,
`40 8a ed be`). That said, a client-controlled DNS answer must never be able to turn a 401 into a
500, and PTR data is arbitrary bytes by nature.

## Suggested fix

Tolerate any failure of this lookup, since it only produces a cosmetic hostname for a log line:

```python
    with suppress(herror, UnicodeDecodeError, OSError):
        remote_host, _, _ = await hass.async_add_executor_job(
            gethostbyaddr, request.remote
        )
```

or equivalently, narrowing by type:

```python
    try:
        remote_host, _, _ = await hass.async_add_executor_job(
            gethostbyaddr, request.remote
        )
    except (herror, UnicodeDecodeError, OSError) as err:
        _LOGGER.debug("Reverse lookup for %s failed: %s", remote_addr, err)
```

(`UnicodeDecodeError` subclasses `ValueError`, so `except (herror, ValueError)` also covers it,
though naming the exception is clearer.) A test can be added cheaply: patch
`socket.gethostbyaddr` (or the exec_job call) to raise `UnicodeDecodeError`, then assert that a
request without credentials still answers `401` and that the failure is logged as a failed login.

## Workaround for anyone hitting this

Make sure the HA host's reverse lookup for LAN clients either resolves cleanly or fails with
`herror`:

- point the HA container/host DNS at a resolver that does **not** forward private PTR queries to the
  broken upstream (we disabled "private reverse DNS servers" in AdGuard Home, after which it returns
  `NXDOMAIN` and HA behaves), or
- add the client addresses to the HA host's `/etc/hosts`, which `gethostbyaddr()` consults before
  DNS, or
- fix/disable the PTR answers on the router itself.

Diagnosis one-liner: an unauthenticated `curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://<ha>:8123/api/`
must print `401`; if it prints `500`, grep the HA log for `process_wrong_login`.

Philips TV permanently reported as off after screenstate fallback fix ### The problem

Description

This appears to be a regression related to #177542 and the fix introduced in #178004.

On my Philips 75MLED910/12, Home Assistant previously reported the TV as permanently on. Since updating to Home Assistant 2026.9.x, it is now permanently reported as off, even while the TV is powered on and displaying content.

Device

  • TV: Philips 75MLED910/12
  • Platform: TPN258E
  • JointSPACE API: 6.1
  • Home Assistant Core: 2026.9.2
  • ha-philipsjs: 3.2.5

Diagnostics

I collected two diagnostic files from the same TV and Home Assistant installation:

  • one while the TV was OFF / in standby
  • one while the TV was definitely ON and displaying content

The relevant values are identical in both states:

  | TV OFF | TV ON -- | -- | -- powerstate | null | null screenstate | "Off" | "Off" on | true | true

Therefore, on this model screenstate does not reflect the actual TV state and cannot reliably be used as a fallback when powerstate is unavailable.

This causes the condition introduced in #178004 (powerstate is None and screenstate == "Off") to classify the TV as off in both states.

The resulting entities are:

  • media_player: permanently off
  • screen switch: permanently off
  • remote entity: permanently on
  • Ambilight entity: works and can be controlled normally

I have attached both diagnostic files for comparison. The only meaningful differences I could find between them are the current activity (context.level1) and the Ambilight configuration; the power-related values above do not change.

Please let me know if additional debug logging or API responses from the TV would be useful.

query:
devolo Home Network: Wi-Fi neighbor scan runs on every setup even though the sensor is disabled, and it knocks Wi-Fi clients off the access point

### The problem

On every setup of a config entry (so on every Home Assistant start), the integration calls `WifiNeighborAPsGet` on devolo devices with Wi-Fi. It does this even when the entity "Neighboring Wi-Fi networks" is disabled, which is its default.

On the device this call triggers a scan of the neighboring Wi-Fi networks. The scan takes about 8.5 seconds on a Magic 1 WiFi 2-1, and sensitive Wi-Fi clients lose their connection to the access point when it finishes. In my setup the Wi-Fi dongle of a GoodWe inverter (Hi-Flying module) dropped off the network about 90 seconds after every Home Assistant start, at the moment the scan result was returned.

Since the entity is disabled by default, I expected no scan to be triggered unless a user enables it.

### Cause

`async_setup_entry()` in `homeassistant/components/devolo_home_network/__init__.py` creates the `DevoloWifiNeighborAPsGetCoordinator` for every device with the `wifi1` feature and then refreshes all coordinators unconditionally:

```python
    for coordinator in coordinators.values():
        await coordinator.async_config_entry_first_refresh()
```

After that the coordinator has no listeners (the entity is disabled), so the scan is not repeated. It is the first refresh that causes the disruption.

### Evidence

Packet capture on the Home Assistant host (devolo device 192.168.68.53, Wi-Fi client 192.168.68.75, polled over UDP every 5 s):

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 11:41:02.648 | HA → devolo: `GET /…/deviceapi/v0/WifiNeighborAPsGet` |
| 11:41:10.761 | Last response of the Wi-Fi client |
| 11:41:10.768 | Next request to the Wi-Fi client is not answered any more, and none after it |
| 11:41:11.121 | devolo → HA: `200 OK` for `WifiNeighborAPsGet` (8.5 s after the request) |

The other calls (`WifiConnectedStationsGet`, `WifiGuestAccessGet`, `LedSettingsGet`) return within 50 to 500 ms and cause no problem.

Three Home Assistant restarts in a row showed the same failure, each 97 to 105 seconds after the start. After I disabled the config entry of this devolo device, the next restart did not disconnect the client.

### Proposed fix

Skip the first refresh of the neighbor coordinator when its entity is disabled in the entity registry, or do not refresh it during setup at all and let the first listener trigger it. I can open a pull request if that approach is fine with you.

### Environment

- Home Assistant Core 2026.9.4, Home Assistant OS 18.3
- devolo Magic 1 WiFi 2-1 (MT 3133), firmware 6.0.1
- Entity "Neighboring Wi-Fi networks": disabled (integration default)

### Integration

devolo Home Network: https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/devolo_home_network

Logging crash ("Thread.__init__() not called") can freeze Core completely until manual restart (Python 3.14)

### The problem

Home Assistant Core sometimes becomes completely unresponsive (no UI, no API, no automations) while Supervisor still reports it as healthy. It stays like this until I manually restart the VM/container — it does not recover on its own and the Supervisor watchdog does not restart it.

With debug logging enabled, I found the trigger: a normal log call (in my case from zeroconf, handling an incoming network packet) fails with this error:

```
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.14/threading.py", line 1143, in name
    assert self._initialized, "Thread.__init__() not called"
AssertionError: Thread.__init__() not called
```

This means some thread in the process was not created the normal way, so Python can't get its name — and logging needs that name for every log line.

The problem snowballs from there: when this error happens, Home Assistant's own error handler tries to log it, hits the exact same error, and loops forever. This eventually crashes Home Assistant's shutdown routine too (homeassistant/util/executor.py, trying to join that same broken thread), so the shutdown never finishes properly either. The result: the event loop is closed, but a couple of background threads (a camera stream and a custom integration's websocket) are still alive and spam errors forever, so the Python process never actually exits — it just becomes a zombie that looks "running" to Supervisor/Docker but answers nothing.

This doesn't seem tied to one specific integration — I first saw the same crash triggered by the Cast integration (see linked issue below), and this time by zeroconf instead, with Cast working fine throughout. I'm running Python 3.14, so I suspect this is a Python 3.14 compatibility issue in Home Assistant's own thread/executor code rather than something integration-specific.

A low-overhead wrapper should therefore be assigned to both: ```python import os import sys import threading import time import homeassistant.util.thread as ha_thread import homeassistant.util.executor as ha_executor _orig_async_raise = ha_thread.async_raise DIAG_FILE = "/config/thread_crash_diag.log" def _raw(obj, attr, default=""): try: return object.__getattribute__(obj, attr) except BaseException as err: return f"" def _append(line): try: fd = os.open(DIAG_FILE, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_APPEND, 0o600) try: os.write(fd, line.encode("utf-8", "backslashreplace")) finally: os.close(fd) except BaseException: pass def _diag_async_raise(tid, exctype): target = threading._active.get(tid) caller = sys._getframe(1) token = time.monotonic_ns() _append( "ASYNC_RAISE BEFORE " f"mono_ns={token} wall_ns={time.time_ns()} " f"tid={tid!r} exc={getattr(exctype, '__name__', repr(exctype))!r} " f"caller={caller.f_code.co_filename}:{caller.f_lineno}:{caller.f_code.co_name} " f"target_id={None if target is None else id(target)!r} " f"target_name={_raw(target, '_name')!r} " f"target_initialized={_raw(target, '_initialized')!r}\n" ) try: result = _orig_async_raise(tid, exctype) except BaseException as err: _append( "ASYNC_RAISE AFTER " f"mono_ns={time.monotonic_ns()} token={token} " f"outcome=raised error={type(err).__name__}:{err!r}\n" ) raise else: _append( "ASYNC_RAISE AFTER " f"mono_ns={time.monotonic_ns()} token={token} outcome=returned\n" ) return result ha_thread.async_raise = _diag_async_raise ha_executor.async_raise = _diag_async_raise ``` I would keep this first pass intentionally small — no full stack formatting before the injection, because that could perturb the timing we are trying to measure. Follow-up on my capture from earlier, and it is about the aftermath rather than the burst. I found this by accident less than an hour after the burst, while installing updates, when every API call to the instance started timing out at 30 seconds. A burst the process survives leaves the `concurrent.futures` executor pool persistently starved, and nothing reports it. `docker inspect` says running with no restarts, there is no exit code line, the supervisor watchdog never complains, and the container log keeps writing perfectly ordinary lines. The only visible symptom is `Updating took longer than the scheduled update interval` from whichever integrations do their polling in the executor, plus a Core API slow enough to time clients out. Thread count on my instance went 89 at the start of the burst, 25 at the floor, still only 58 fifty minutes later, and 104 immediately after a restart. It does not self-heal. The reason I think this matters for the issue rather than just for my box: it appears to be what connects a survivable burst to a later freeze. Over the last 30 days, 692 of 720 hours on my instance had exactly zero of those warnings, five hours had single-poll noise of 1 to 9, and the rest belong to two episodes that both sit right after a burst. The first one is the interesting one. On 2026-08-27 a burst fired at 14:07:01 and the process survived it. From 15:00 that day until 11:00 the next morning the warnings ran at a steady 120 per hour, about two a minute, for 21 hours straight. They stop exactly at 10:26:41 on 2026-08-28, which is when that instance froze and the watchdog restarted it at 10:31:02. I had recorded those two as separate events roughly 20 hours apart. They are not separate: the decay starts with the burst, runs continuously, and terminates in the freeze. That also explains something about the freeze that had bothered me. Its dying run had 744 `cannot wait/notify on un-acquired lock` errors and zero `Thread.__init__() not called`. If the pool had been starving for 20 hours by then, `_adjust_thread_count` and `_idle_semaphore.acquire` are exactly where the work was piling up, so the lock surface is where it surfaced and the logging surface never got a look in. My 2026-09-10 burst did the same thing at the same rate, 121 warnings in the first hour and 51 in the next, and the only reason it did not end the same way is that I deliberately restarted about an hour in. So the same starting condition has produced both a survivable event and a freeze on my instance, and what decided it looks like how long the pool was left starving rather than anything about the burst itself. Worth noting the corollary: my 2026-09-02 burst logged only 9 warnings in its hour because the watchdog killed Core under three minutes in, so a low count means a short event, not a mild one. @Profil404 this may be the difference between your 09-08 capture and mine, and checking it needs no new instrumentation, which I know is where you had got to. Yours was MainThread-only and fatal where mine were MainThread-only and survivable, and if the outcome is set by how long the executor is left degraded rather than by which threads took the hits, then that difference stops being mysterious: your instance may just have been further along, or had less headroom to absorb it. It is worth grepping your own logs for `took longer than the scheduled update interval` in the hours between a burst and the freeze that followed. If those hours are full of it, this is the same mechanism, and the practical consequence is that a restart soon after a burst is what saves the instance. @elupus on your point that the initial fault is what matters and the rest is side effects, agreed for root cause, and the lock misread being first is what my last comment showed. This is about the other half of the question: the side effects are what actually cost you the instance, and they run for hours rather than seconds, which is why I keep counting them. This capture changes where I think the investigation belongs. The first abnormal event is not the `Thread.__init__() not called` assertion. It is the executor worker failing in `Condition.notify()` with `cannot notify on un-acquired lock`. The Thread assertion follows while Python is trying to log that failure. The dead workers, pool starvation, API delays, and later freeze are downstream consequences. I don't think the three failures should be treated as ordinary independent bugs anymore. During the same short burst, `_initialized` disagreed with the object's raw state, a newly created asyncio Future failed its Future protocol check, and a Condition rejected a lock that should have been owned. A shared transient interpreter/runtime-state problem is now the strongest working hypothesis. That still isn't proof of a stale `LOAD_ATTR` cache or a CPython-only bug. The Future trace does not show which part of `isfuture()` failed, and the Condition path involves a real lock operation. For a transient wrong attribute read I would treat every one of those as potentially load bearing rather than incidental: PGO and LTO inline and reorder aggressively, musl's pthread and TLS implementation is not glibc's, and mimalloc changes object reuse patterns. query:
Hydrawise: TransportQueryError from get_user is not caught, whole controller goes unavailable and logs as unexpected error

### The problem

The Hydrawise coordinator does not catch errors raised by `pydrawise` inside `_async_update_data`. When Hunter's GraphQL API answers the `me` query with an error payload instead of data, `gql.transport.exceptions.TransportQueryError` escapes the coordinator as an unexpected exception. `DataUpdateCoordinator` then logs it as `Unexpected error fetching hydrawise data` with a full traceback, and every Hydrawise entity on the entry goes `unavailable` until the next poll.

`get_user()` is the first statement in `_async_update_data` (`coordinator.py` line 98 on `dev` today), and there is no `try/except` around it. So a single transient upstream error takes the whole controller unavailable, and it is logged as an unexpected error rather than as an ordinary `UpdateFailed`.

Observed on one installation over about 45 hours with debug logging enabled: 1 failure in 362 polls (about 0.3%). It recovered on the next poll (`Fetching hydrawise data recovered`). No HTTP 429, DNS or authentication errors appeared anywhere in the core log. The failing call was a real network fetch, not a throttled cache hit, so this is not the client-side rate limiter.

**Suggested fix:** wrap the `pydrawise` calls in `_async_update_data` and re-raise transport or query errors as `UpdateFailed`, so a transient upstream error is logged as an update failure and not as an unexpected exception.

### What version of Home Assistant Core has the issue?

core-2026.9.3 (the code on `dev` is unchanged at the time of writing)

### What was the last working version of Home Assistant Core?

Unknown

### What type of installation are you running?

Home Assistant OS

### Integration causing the issue

Hunter Hydrawise

### Link to integration documentation on our website

https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/hydrawise

### Anything in the logs that might be useful for us?

```txt
ERROR (MainThread) [homeassistant.components.hydrawise.coordinator] Unexpected error fetching hydrawise data
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../homeassistant/helpers/update_coordinator.py", ..., in _async_refresh
  File ".../homeassistant/components/hydrawise/coordinator.py", line 98, in _async_update_data
    data = HydrawiseData(user=await self.api.get_user(fetch_zones=False))
  File ".../pydrawise/hybrid.py", line 117, in get_user
  File ".../pydrawise/client.py", line 94, in _query
gql.transport.exceptions.TransportQueryError: {'message': 'unavailable'}
```

Occurrence: 2026-09-20 02:04:47 UTC. Entities went `unavailable` at 02:04:47.654 and recovered at 02:09:48.005, exactly one poll interval later.

### Additional information

A separate, more frequent cause of whole-controller unavailability on the same install is expected behavior, not a bug: `entity.py` uses `available = super().available and self.controller.online`. When the controller loses its own link to Hunter's cloud, every entity goes unavailable while every poll still succeeds, and nothing is logged. Windows of 5 to 55 minutes were seen. I mention it only so the two are not confused. This report is only about the uncaught `TransportQueryError`.

### The problem

`GoogleGenerativeAISttEntity.async_process_audio_stream` in `homeassistant/components/google_generative_ai_conversation/stt.py` only logs an error inside its `except (APIError, ClientError, ValueError)` block. If the API call succeeds (HTTP 200, no exception) but `response.text` is falsy, the code falls through to `return stt.SpeechResult(None, stt.SpeechResultState.ERROR)` with no log line at all.

I hit this in testing the newly released [`gemini-3.5-transcribe`](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/models/gemini-3.5-transcribe). It consistently returns `finishReason: STOP` with zero output tokens for valid audio. With this integration's current STT error handling, that failure mode no zero log output.

### Suggested fix

Add an `else` branch (or a check after the `try`) that logs a warning when `response.text` is falsy, for example `LOGGER.warning("STT model returned no text (finish_reason=%s)", ...)`, mirroring the `LOGGER.error("Error during STT: %s", err)` already present for the exception case.

Google Generative AI

_No response_

Found while investigating why the new `gemini-3.5-transcribe` model did not work (See also #180388).

query:
Raise HomeAssistantError when acaia button actions fail

### Description

The `acaia` integration (platinum) marks the `action-exceptions` quality scale rule as `exempt` ("No custom actions are defined"), but the rule also covers platform entity actions:

> This rule is not limited to custom service actions registered by the integration. Platform actions (for example, switching a `switch` or turning on a `light`) count towards this rule as well and should raise an exception when they encounter a failure.

The exemption only applies to integrations without custom actions and with only read-only platforms. `acaia` has button entities (tare, reset timer, start/stop timer).

**Gap:** `AcaiaButton.async_press` (`homeassistant/components/acaia/button.py`) calls `press_fn(self._scale)` without error handling. When writing to the scale fails, aioacaia raises `AcaiaError` / `AcaiaDeviceNotFound` (`aioacaia/scale.py` `_write_msg`), which reaches the action caller as a raw library exception.

**Expected outcome:**
- Catch the aioacaia errors in `async_press` and raise a translated `HomeAssistantError` (new entry under `exceptions` in `strings.json`)
- Add tests for a failed button press
- Change `action-exceptions` from `exempt` to `done` in `quality_scale.yaml`

### Additional context

- Rule: https://developers.home-assistant.io/docs/core/integration-quality-scale/rules/action-exceptions
- Found during an audit of integrations marking `action-exceptions` as exempt; compliant integrations were switched to `done` in #183997, #183998, #183999 and #184000, and non-compliant bronze / no-tier integrations to `todo` in #184005 and #184004
- Code owner: @zweckj
patch:
diff --git a/homeassistant/components/acaia/button.py b/homeassistant/components/acaia/button.py
index 12093309237..4a3c6ff0cee 100644
--- a/homeassistant/components/acaia/button.py
+++ b/homeassistant/components/acaia/button.py
@@ -61,4 +61,5 @@ class AcaiaButton(AcaiaEntity, ButtonEntity):
     @override
     async def async_press(self) -> None:
         """Handle the button press."""
+        # aioacaia queues button commands, so enqueueing cannot fail.
         await self.entity_description.press_fn(self._scale)

Google Generative AI: ThinkingConfig is never sent for Gemma models, so thinking_level "minimal" is ignored (Gemma 4 ~9 s instead of ~1.2 s)

### The problem

When a Google Generative AI conversation subentry uses a Gemma model (e.g. `models/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it`), the integration never passes a `ThinkingConfig` to the API, regardless of the configured *Thinking budget* / *Thinking level* options. On the Gemini API Gemma 4 thinks by default, so every Assist request spends 240–400 thinking tokens and takes 6–11 s. Sending `thinkingLevel: minimal` brings the same request down to ~1.2 s with a correct tool call — but there is no way to make the integration send it.

**Cause (code):** `_create_thinking_config()` in `homeassistant/components/google_generative_ai_conversation/entity.py` returns `None` unless `_is_thinking_model()` is true, and that helper only accepts model names starting with `gemini-2.5` / `gemini-3` (lines 99–111 in 2026.9.1; unchanged on `dev`). `_is_gemini_3_model()` gates the `thinking_level` map the same way, so Gemma models fall through both checks.

**What I measured** (same API key, direct `generateContent` calls to `gemma-4-26b-a4b-it`):

| Request | Latency | `thoughtsTokenCount` |
|---|---|---|
| short question, default config | 6.65 s / 6.90 s | 237 / 271 |
| `thinkingConfig.thinkingBudget: 0` | HTTP 400 "Thinking budget is not supported for this model" | – |
| `thinkingConfig.thinkingLevel: "minimal"` | **1.45 s** | 0 |
| `thinkingConfig.thinkingLevel: "low"` | HTTP 400 "Thinking level is not supported for this model" | – |
| Assist-sized system prompt (67 exposed entities + Assist tools, 4 143 prompt tokens), `thinkingLevel: "minimal"` | **1.23 s**, correct `functionCall` | 0 |
| same prompt, default config | 9.15 s (and the reasoning leaked into the text part) | 397 |

Through Home Assistant (`conversation/process` on the same agent, with `thinking_level: minimal` and `thinking_budget: -1` stored in the subentry and verified in `.storage/core.config_entries`): 8.9–11.1 s per request, i.e. the default-thinking behaviour. The existing Gemini agent on the same instance (`gemini-3.1-flash-lite`, recommended settings) answers the same questions in 1.0–1.5 s, so the slow path is specific to Gemma.

**What I expected:** either Gemma models are treated as thinking models that accept `thinkingLevel` (`minimal` works; `low/medium/high` and `thinkingBudget` are rejected by the API for `gemma-4-26b-a4b-it`), or the integration sends `ThinkingLevel.MINIMAL` by default for Gemma so that a voice-assistant pipeline is usable. A minimal change would be to include `gemma-4` in `_is_thinking_model()` / `_is_gemini_3_model()` (or a dedicated `_is_gemma_model()` that maps only `"minimal"`).
