### 🐛 Describe the bug ### Summary For Python-only builds, vLLM resolves a precompiled-wheel variant before fetching wheel metadata. The [Python-only build documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/getting_started/installation/gpu/) documents `VLLM_PRECOMPILED_WHEEL_VARIANT` as selecting a variant subdirectory such as `cu129` or `cu130`. If it is not set, the CUDA variant is auto-detected from the local environment using PyTorch or `nvidia-smi`. The [nightly wheel documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/contributing/ci/nightly_builds/) describes the root index as the default variant and named subdirectories as variant-specific indices. If metadata for the selected variant cannot be fetched, [`precompiled_wheel_utils.determine_wheel_url()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/836aac92ffdaa337083934181cb6d00b64b2a1a6/setup.py) currently retries the root/default metadata: ```python try: wheels, repo_url = precompiled_wheel_utils.fetch_metadata_for_variant( commit, variant ) except Exception as e: logger.warning( "Failed to fetch precompiled wheel metadata for variant %s: %s", variant, e, ) try_default = True if try_default: print("Trying the default variant from remote") wheels, repo_url = precompiled_wheel_utils.fetch_metadata_for_variant( commit, None ) ``` The fallback is part of the current resolution order. The issue is that once it happens, the CUDA variant selected explicitly or detected from the local environment is no longer used to qualify the fallback wheel. The wheel filtering that follows checks the package name and target architecture: ```python if wheel.get("package_name") == "vllm" and arch in wheel.get( "platform_tag", "" ): ... ``` but does not check that the root/default artifact matches the CUDA variant selected earlier. I encountered a concrete case where PyTorch CUDA 12.9 selected `cu129`, the `cu129` metadata lookup failed, and the fallback selected a native artifact requiring CUDA 13. I propose keeping the selected CUDA variant for the rest of precompiled-wheel resolution: if its metadata cannot be fetched, propagate that lookup failure instead of retrying the root/default variant. ### Concrete reproduction I encountered this while reproducing a separate issue from the exact v0.27.1 source: ```text source: v0.27.1 6e448d0ea9bf3d88d898b65449ca6dc2aec170ac PyTorch: 2.13.0+cu129 torch.version.cuda: 12.9 ``` Using the documented Python-only precompiled installation path: ```bash VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 uv pip install -e . --torch-backend=auto ``` with neither `VLLM_PRECOMPILED_WHEEL_VARIANT` nor `VLLM_PRECOMPILED_WHEEL_COMMIT` set, the CUDA detection path selected: ```text cu129 ``` The Python-only build selected the following precompiled base commit: ```text f5bb701fa270f5c801f1572e1478b56f292d8dfc ``` For that commit, metadata for `cu129` was unavailable: ```text https://wheels.vllm.ai/f5bb701fa270f5c801f1572e1478b56f292d8dfc/cu129/vllm/metadata.json -> 404 ``` The fallback then queried the root/default metadata: ```text https://wheels.vllm.ai/f5bb701fa270f5c801f1572e1478b56f292d8dfc/vllm/metadata.json -> 200 ``` The resulting path was: ```text PyTorch CUDA 12.9 -> select cu129 -> cu129 metadata unavailable -> retry root/default metadata -> select default wheel ``` ### Artifact verification I extracted `vllm/_C_stable_libtorch.abi3.so` from the wheel selected through the root/default fallback and inspected its ELF dependencies. The fallback artifact requires: ```text NEEDED: libcudart.so.13 ``` As a control, the published `cu129` artifact for the exact v0.27.1 commit is available at: ```text https://wheels.vllm.ai/6e448d0ea9bf3d88d898b65449ca6dc2aec170ac/cu129/vllm/metadata.json -> 200 ``` Its `_C_stable_libtorch.abi3.so` requires: ```text NEEDED: libcudart.so.12 ``` So in this reproduction, the resolver first selected `cu129`, then replaced that selection after the metadata failure with a root/default artifact requiring `libcudart.so.13`. The exact-v0.27.1 `cu129` artifact is only used here as a control for the native CUDA dependency of a published `cu129` wheel. I am not proposing any change to the existing base-commit selection behavior. The problematic transition happens after the base commit and CUDA variant have already been selected. ### Why the default fallback is unsafe The [nightly wheel documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/contributing/ci/nightly_builds/) treats the root index as the default variant and named subdirectories as separate variants. It also notes that the default variant can have a named alias, and that not every variant is present on every commit. A missing `cu129` index therefore does not imply that the root/default wheel is an equivalent `cu129` replacement. The current fallback nevertheless changes: ```text selected: cu129 | | metadata lookup fails v fallback: root/default | | package + architecture filtering v selected wheel ``` There is no CUDA-variant check between the selected variant and the fallback artifact. This affects explicit selection as well as auto-detection. For example, a user setting: ```text VLLM_PRECOMPILED_WHEEL_VARIANT=cu129 ``` can currently receive the default variant if the `cu129` metadata lookup fails. The root/default CUDA variant also cannot be inferred safely from the current `VLLM_MAIN_CUDA_VERSION`. `VLLM_PRECOMPILED_WHEEL_COMMIT` can select a different or historical wheel commit, and the normal Python-only path can select a base commit from `main`. The default artifact for that commit may therefore reflect a different CUDA build configuration from the one selected in the current environment. With the current metadata and wheel filtering, there is no check that makes the root/default wheel a verified replacement for an already selected CUDA variant. ### Proposed fix For CUDA, once a variant has been selected, fetch metadata only for that variant. If: ```python fetch_metadata_for_variant(commit, variant) ``` fails, propagate that error instead of retrying: ```python fetch_metadata_for_variant(commit, None) ``` The behavior changes from: ```text current: select cu129 -> fetch cu129 metadata -> lookup fails -> fetch root/default metadata -> select by package name / architecture ``` to: ```text proposed: select cu129 -> fetch cu129 metadata -> lookup fails -> propagate the original lookup failure ``` A fallback could be kept if the resolver had enough information to verify that the default artifact is compatible with the selected CUDA variant. That check does not exist in the current resolution path, so doing that safely would require a broader metadata or compatibility-selection change. The proposed patch instead keeps the existing variant selection intact and fails at the variant-specific lookup when that artifact is unavailable. A root/default wheel may happen to be compatible in some cases, but the current resolver cannot distinguish those cases from the incompatible case reproduced above. The existing base-commit selection is unchanged, and the ROCm precompiled-wheel path is unchanged. Regression coverage checks both CUDA selection paths: - explicit `VLLM_PRECOMPILED_WHEEL_VARIANT`; - auto-detected CUDA variant. In both cases, a failed selected-variant lookup should propagate its original error without calling `fetch_metadata_for_variant(commit, None)`. ### Current `main` The same fallback is still present on `main` at [`836aac92ffdaa337083934181cb6d00b64b2a1a6`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/836aac92ffdaa337083934181cb6d00b64b2a1a6). I also reproduced the path independently of the current contents of `wheels.vllm.ai` with a metadata-fetch stub: ```text fetch(commit, "cu129") -> raises fetch(commit, None) -> returns default metadata ``` On the unmodified code, both explicit and auto-detected `cu129` make both calls and return the default wheel. The regression test for the proposed behavior expects the first lookup error to propagate instead. ### Context / related work The variant-specific lookup followed by the default fallback was introduced in #29838. #32948 later added CUDA variant auto-detection while retaining that fallback. Related reports cover different paths: - #42338 reports a similar CUDA 12.9 -> CUDA 13 result through package resolver/index selection. This issue concerns the Python-only precompiled-wheel fallback after a CUDA variant has already been selected. - #49683 concerns availability of `cu129` nightly artifacts. Missing variant-specific metadata can trigger the fallback described here, but artifact availability itself is a separate problem. - PR #34139 discussed native compatibility concerns when falling back across different nightly commits. Here the wheel commit stays fixed while the selected CUDA variant is replaced by that commit's default variant. I have a patch implementing the proposed behavior with regression coverage for both explicit and auto-detected CUDA variants, and will open a draft PR shortly. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

query:
Multi-node startup deadlock in in_the_same_node_as() gloo barrier at 2 nodes x TP-16 with the Ray executor (regression between 0.26.1rc1.dev78 and 0.26.1rc1.dev148)

## Summary

Starting a 2-node, TP-16 deployment of DeepSeek-R1 (FP8) with the Ray distributed executor deadlocks during distributed initialization. All 16 ranks start, but the gloo barrier inside `in_the_same_node_as()` never completes. The process sits idle for exactly 30 minutes and then dies on the gloo TCP deadline:

```
RuntimeError: Application timeout caused pair closure
[.../gloo/transport/tcp/unbound_buffer.cc:78] Timed out waiting 1800000ms for recv operation to complete
```

The traceback is identical on every reproduction:

```
parallel_state.py:1838 initialize_model_parallel
  -> :2009 ensure_model_parallel_initialized
  -> :1328 init_model_parallel_group
  -> :519  __init__
  -> shm_broadcast.py:1022 create_from_process_group
  -> :2267 in_the_same_node_as
  -> distributed_c10d.py:5356 barrier
```

The same configuration on a **single node** works. The failure requires two nodes, and it reproduces on hosts with no NVLink fabric between them (InfiniBand only, non-MNNVL).

## Regression range

This is a regression, not an unsupported configuration. Using the per-commit wheels at `https://wheels.vllm.ai/<sha>/`, with the container base image, model, flags and every non-vLLM dependency held byte-identical across arms (`torch 2.13.0+cu130`, `torchvision 0.28.0+cu130`, `flashinfer-python`/`flashinfer-cubin` `0.6.15.post1`, `flashinfer-jit-cache 0.6.15.post1+cu130`), six commits were scored:

| Commit | Version | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `35efdf6b3` | `0.26.1rc1.dev34` | pass |
| `6f00a1ae3` | `0.26.1rc1.dev78` | **pass (last known good)** |
| `5f8f72866` | `0.26.1rc1.dev148` | **hang (first known bad)** |
| `0eec856cc` | `0.26.1rc1.dev156` | hang |
| `92643d68f` | `0.26.1rc1.dev195` | hang |
| `0cf49a5d1` | `0.26.1rc1.dev276` | hang |

At the release level, `v0.26.0` is good and `v0.27.0` is bad, and the failure still reproduces on current `main` after `v0.27.1`.

The bisect stops at `(6f00a1ae3, 5f8f72866]` because the 69 commits in between publish only `manylinux_2_28_aarch64` wheels and no `cp38-abi3` `x86_64` wheel, so they cannot be scored on this hardware. Checked at `<sha>/`, `<sha>/vllm/`, `<sha>/cu130/` and `<sha>/cu130/vllm/` for an interior commit against a control commit that does publish x86_64, to rule out a path mistake on our side.

## What the evidence rules out

- **Not a change to `in_the_same_node_as` itself.** The function's source is byte-identical across the whole bracket (SHA-256 of `inspect.getsource` matches on all six arms, 92 lines). Whatever regressed alters *which ranks reach the barrier, and when* — the calling context — not this function's code.
- **Not the kernel libraries.** Rebuilding a bad-side arm with the good-side `flashinfer-python 0.6.15.post1` still hangs, so the flashinfer / tvm-ffi / tilelang bundle is not the carrier. `torch`, `torchvision`, `triton`, NCCL and the CUDA toolkit are identical on both sides of the boundary.
- **Not shared-memory exhaustion.** `No available shared memory broadcast block` never appears; the count is zero on every arm.
- **Not infrastructure.** Both nodes are present and communicating in every failing run (two distinct worker IPs in the logs), and the identical allocation passes on good commits.
- **Not custom all-reduce, and not an MNNVL-specific path** — these hosts have no NVLink fabric between nodes.
- **Red herrings.** The logs lead with `ImportError: .../deep_ep_cpp...: undefined symbol: _ZN3c104impl3cow23materialize_cow_storageERNS_11StorageImplE`, plus a post-timeout `ray.exceptions.ActorHandleNotFoundError` cascade at `ray_executor_v2.py:566` and `Engine core initialization failed`. None of it is causal: **the same `deep_ep_cpp` ImportErrors appear in the runs that pass**, and the Ray errors are teardown after the deadline fires.

## Reproduction

2 nodes x 8 H100 (80 GB), InfiniBand interconnect, no inter-node NVLink, Ray executor:

```
vllm serve <deepseek-r1-fp8-checkpoint> \
  --tensor-parallel-size 16 \
  --pipeline-parallel-size 1 \
  --data-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-model-len 4096 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --block-size 128 \
  --load-format runai_streamer \
  --distributed-executor-backend ray
```

Expected: the server initializes and serves. Actual: startup hangs in `in_the_same_node_as`, then dies ~30 minutes later on the gloo deadline.

## Notes

One candidate worth ruling out early: `435c4dad9` (#50311, "[ROCm][CI] Avoid Ray worker startup env race") sits in the unscorable window and its title matches the implicated area, but its diff touches only `requirements/test/rocm.in` and `requirements/test/rocm.txt` and ships no runtime code, so it is not the cause. No commit in the window is being asserted as the culprit — the remaining commits could not be scored for lack of x86_64 artifacts.

Happy to run a specific candidate commit, a patch, or additional diagnostics on the 2-node setup if that would help narrow the 69-commit window.

[Bug]: Out-of-vocab stop_token_ids crashes the whole engine on backends with bounds-checked index kernels (single-request DoS)

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`stop_token_ids` is not validated against the vocabulary size. An out-of-vocab token id in a request is accepted unchecked and is later used as a **logits index on the device** (e.g. min_tokens / EOS masking does `logits.index_put_((rows, all_stop_token_ids), -inf)` in `vllm/v1/sample/logits_processor/builtin.py`). On backends whose index kernels perform device-side bounds checking, a single such request crashes the entire engine with an unrecoverable device exception.

Reproduced end-to-end on vLLM 0.23.0 + vllm-ascend 0.23.0rc1, DeepSeek-V4-Flash (vocab 129280), PD-disaggregated deployment (MooncakeHybridConnector + MTP), CANN 9.1.0:

```
# request
{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}], "stop_token_ids": [151645], "max_tokens": 300}

# device error (all 8 TP ranks die simultaneously)
Index out of range in dimension 1: index value 151645 exceeds bounds 129280!
[ASSERT] .../ascendc/index_check/index_check.h:130: Assertion `(idx < bound)' failed.
fault kernel_name=IndexCheck_int32_high_performance_1
RuntimeError: vector core exception, retCode=0x31
```

The prefill instance dies completely (HTTP 500 for all subsequent requests). 151645 is `<|im_end|>` of the older DeepSeek V3 tokenizer; DeepSeek-V4-Flash's vocab is 129280, so clients reusing stale token ids hit this trivially.

Trigger conditions (all verified experimentally):
1. `stop_token_ids` contains an id `>= vocab_size` — passes `_verify_common` which only checks the type (`vllm/sampling_params.py`)
2. The id reaches a device-side indexing path. This happens whenever `min_tokens > 0` (`MinTokensLogitsProcessor.apply` / `apply_with_spec_decode` register `params.all_stop_token_ids` and index logits with them). Note the PD proxy example scripts rewrite prefill requests to `max_tokens=1, min_tokens=1` (`load_balance_proxy_server_example.py`), which activates this path for **every** request going through the proxy
3. Backend performs bounds checking on index ops (Ascend CANN 9.1.x inserts IndexCheck kernels; older CANN 9.0.1 silently corrupts neighboring logits instead — arguably worse)

On CUDA the same request "works" only because out-of-bounds `index_put_` semantics are luck-dependent; on NPU with CANN 9.1 it is a guaranteed device-level crash. Either way the id can never match a sampled token, so rejecting it upfront loses nothing.

`logit_bias` and `allowed_token_ids` are already validated against the vocabulary in `SamplingParams.verify()`; `stop_token_ids` is the one unchecked entry point into `all_stop_token_ids`.

### Proposed fix

Add `_validate_stop_token_ids` to `SamplingParams` mirroring `_validate_logit_bias`, rejecting out-of-vocab ids with a 400 before the request reaches the engine. PR to follow.

Downstream issue: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/issues/15200

[Perf] BF16x3 router GEMM gated off family-120 Blackwell (GB10 / DGX Spark, sm_121) — the only barrier for DeepSeek-V4-Flash's fp32 router

**Summary**

On NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark, compute capability (12, 1) → family 120), every specialized MoE router GEMM tier in `gate_linear.py` is disabled by the Hopper / family-100 capability gate. For **DeepSeek-V4-Flash** specifically (router shape `hidden_size=4096, n_routed_experts=256`, fp32 router weights via `force_fp32_compute`), the other tiers carry independent barriers (bf16-weight requirement, hidden-size list, shape allow-list), which leaves **BF16x3 (#47973) as the only applicable tier — blocked solely by `is_device_capability_family(100)`**, even though this shape satisfies its only dimensional constraint (`input_size % 8 == 0`).

**Details** (v0.26.0, `vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/router/gate_linear.py`)

The arch gate (:59-63):

```python
is_hopper = current_platform.is_device_capability((9, 0))
is_blackwell = current_platform.is_device_capability_family(100)
can_use_specialized_kernels = (
    current_platform.is_cuda() and (is_hopper or is_blackwell) and not bias)
```

`is_device_capability_family()` computes `capability.to_int() // 10 == capability // 10`, so GB10 gives `121 // 10 = 12 != 10` → `is_blackwell = False`.

Tier-by-tier for DeepSeek-V4-Flash (router: 4096 → 256 experts, fp32 weights, fp32 logits, `scoring_func="sqrtsoftplus"`):

- **Tier 1, cuteDSL `ll_bf16_gemm` (#42562):** requires bf16 *weights*. Ours are fp32 — `force_fp32_compute` sets `params_dtype = torch.float32` precisely *because* `can_use_specialized_kernels` is False (on supported archs the weights stay bf16). Blocked by the arch gate first, dtype second.
- **Tier 2, DSV3 specialized GEMM:** `DSV3_SUPPORTED_HIDDEN_SIZES = [7168, 6144]` — 4096 is not covered.
- **Tier 3, FP32 router GEMV (#48335):** `FP32_SUPPORTED_SHAPES = {(3072, 256), (6144, 128), (6144, 256)}` — (4096, 256) is not covered.
- **BF16x3 (#47973):** requires `not bias and weight.dtype == torch.float32 and is_cuda() and is_blackwell and input_size % 8 == 0 and enable_bf16x3_router_gemm`. Every condition is satisfiable on GB10 (4096 % 8 == 0) **except `is_blackwell`**. Net result today: the DSv4-Flash router runs as a plain fp32 `F.linear` at every one of its 43 MoE layers.

Meanwhile `vllm/utils/deep_gemm.py:41-45` already treats family 120 as Blackwell for its E8M0 auto-disable check:

```python
if not (current_platform.is_device_capability_family(100)
        or current_platform.is_device_capability_family(120)):
    return False
```

so the codebase is inconsistent about whether family 120 counts as Blackwell for kernel eligibility.

**Question**

Is the family-100 gate on the BF16x3 router GEMM deliberate for sm_121 (numerics, TMA / cubin / thread-block-cluster assumptions that genuinely don't hold on GB10), or is family 120 simply not on the radar? If there is no fundamental blocker, I am happy to benchmark a relaxed gate (`is_device_capability_family(100) or is_device_capability_family(120)`, plus `enable_bf16x3_router_gemm`) on 2× DGX Spark (GB10, aarch64, TP=2 over RoCEv2, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark 284B MoE / 13B active) and report before/after numbers. On GB10's unified-memory bandwidth envelope, the per-token-per-layer fp32 router GEMM is plausibly worth more than on datacenter parts.

query:
NVFP4 MoE silently folds an uninitialised activation scale for weight-only checkpoints (zeroes every expert)

### Summary

`ModelOptNvFp4FusedMoE` accepts a **weight-only** NVFP4 checkpoint (one with
`"input_activations": null` and no `input_scale` tensors) and then folds an
**uninitialised** parameter into the dequantisation alphas. Every expert output is
multiplied by zero, the model degenerates to a single repeated token, and there is
no error and no warning.

The NVFP4 *linear* methods refuse the same checkpoint explicitly. The inconsistency
is the bug.

### Detail

`ModelOptNvFp4FusedMoE.create_weights` registers:

```python
w13_input_scale = PerTensorScaleParameter(
    data=torch.empty(global_sf_num_experts, dtype=torch.float32), ...)
```

A weight-only checkpoint never fills it. `process_weights_after_loading` passes it
straight into the kernel-format conversion, where it becomes both the
dequantisation alpha (`g1_alphas = weight_scale_2 * input_scale`) and the
activation global scale (`a1_gscale = 1.0 / input_scale`).

Observed value in practice: **0.0**. So `g1_alphas` is 0 for every expert, the
whole mixture of experts contributes nothing, and the model runs on attention plus
the shared expert alone.

Both NVFP4 linear methods guard this case:

```python
if not self.quant_config.is_checkpoint_nvfp4_serialized:
    raise ValueError("NVFP4 quantization was selected, "
                     "dynamic quantization is not supported.")
```

and there is a dedicated weight-only linear path
(`ModelOptNvFp4W4A16LinearMethod`). There is **no W4A16 equivalent for MoE** and no
such guard.

### Why this reads as architecture-specific but is not

Reports of this symptom on GB10 / DGX Spark conclude "FLASHINFER_CUTLASS MoE
produces silent garbage on GB10, use marlin". Marlin dequantises the weights and
runs an ordinary bf16 GEMM, so it never consumes an activation scale and never
reaches this code path. The trigger is the checkpoint, not the GPU.

A standalone harness driving `flashinfer.fused_moe.cutlass_fused_moe` directly on
GB10 shows the kernel itself is correct when fed properly, matching an fp32
reference at `cos = 0.9969` (fp4 noise). It also confirms vLLM's
`reorder_w1w3_to_w3w1` and its alpha convention are both correct, so the kernel and
the layout are not at fault.

### Reproduce

Any weight-only modelopt NVFP4 MoE checkpoint. Example:
[`LibertAIDAI/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4`](https://huggingface.co/LibertAIDAI/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4)

```
*.weight_scale   : 37152 tensors
*.weight_scale_2 : 37152 tensors
*.input_scale    : 0 tensors
quantization_config: {"input_activations": null, "quant_algo": "NVFP4", ...}
```

Serve with `--moe-backend flashinfer_cutlass`: every prompt returns one token
repeated to the limit. Serve with `--moe-backend marlin`: output is correct.

### Suggested fix

Any of, in rough order of preference:

1. Add a weight-only MoE path that derives the activation scale dynamically.
   SGLang does this, which is why it serves the same checkpoint correctly.
2. Apply the guard the linear methods already have, so the checkpoint is refused
   loudly rather than served wrongly.
3. At minimum, initialise the parameter to 1.0 instead of `torch.empty`. The
   activation scale cancels analytically (activations are quantised with
   `1/input_scale` and dequantised with an alpha proportional to `input_scale`), so
   it only affects how well activations fit fp4's range through the e4m3 block
   scales. That turns a silent numerical fault into, at worst, a suboptimal one.

### Environment

Reproduced on 2× GB10 (sm_121), TP=2, vLLM `0.1.dev20051+g487ecf187`, flashinfer
0.6.17. Analysis and the standalone MoE harness:
https://github.com/Libertai/glm53-flash-vllm-gb10

[Bug]: --mm-processor-kwargs cannot scope an override to one modality: videos_kwargs is ignored by profiling while a flat "size" leaks into the image budget (Qwen3-VL)

## Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

```
OS                : Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (x86_64)
Python            : 3.12.3
PyTorch           : 2.13.0+cu130
CUDA runtime      : 13.0.88
Nvidia driver     : 580.126.20
GPU               : NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB)
vLLM              : 0.27.2rc1.dev193+gaa9903490 (nightly image for aa9903490)
```

Code paths are unchanged on current main (verified at 7ddb50788).

</details>

## 🐛 Describe the bug

The Qwen3.8 / Qwen3-VL model card's "Long Video Understanding" recipe raises the
**video** processor's pixel budget (`size.longest_edge` from 25,165,824 to
469,762,048, i.e. ~12K to ~224K video tokens). The natural way to apply a
processor override in vLLM is `--mm-processor-kwargs`, and per the review
guidance in #52754, that flag is meant to correspond directly to what the HF
processor accepts. The HF processor does accept a modality-scoped form:
`Qwen3VLProcessor._merge_kwargs` honors
`videos_kwargs={"size": ...}` and applies it to videos only (verified against
transformers 5.x). But vLLM cannot express this override safely in either form:

1. **Scoped form is silently ignored by vLLM's own reads.**
   `--mm-processor-kwargs '{"videos_kwargs": {"size": ...}}'` passes CLI
   validation and reaches the HF processor call (it survives the
   `allow_var_kwargs` filter in `call_hf_processor`), but every place vLLM
   consults mm kwargs itself — `get_max_video_tokens`, the dummy-input builder,
   the data parser's per-item size overrides in `qwen3_vl.py` — only reads the
   flat namespace. Result: encoder-cache profiling reserves for a ~12K-token
   max item while runtime processing can legitimately produce ~229K-token
   items. That is the known under-reservation failure class (encoder cache
   starvation / livelock, cf. #51603).

2. **Flat form leaks across modalities.** `--mm-processor-kwargs '{"size":
   {"longest_edge": 469762048, ...}}'` does lift the video budget, but the same
   flat key is read by the image paths and passed to the image processor, so
   the maximum image item goes from ~16K to ~448K tokens. Observed at boot:

   ```
   Encoder cache will be initialized with a budget of 458752 tokens, and profiled with 1 image items of the maximum feature size.
   ```

   Profiling then runs a 448K-token image dummy through the vision encoder
   (grinds for minutes, and with the default processor cache it aborts boot,
   see #52835).

So the only working way to apply the model card's own recipe today is to edit
`video_preprocessor_config.json` inside the cached checkpoint, which is not
reproducible from serve config and silently reverts on re-download.

### Reproduction (CPU-only, no GPU needed)

```python
from vllm.config import ModelConfig
from vllm.multimodal import MULTIMODAL_REGISTRY

def probe(mm_kwargs, label):
    mc = ModelConfig(model="Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8", mm_processor_kwargs=mm_kwargs)
```

query:
[Bug]: PD Multi Tier supplies nothing when the producer already holds the blocks

### Summary

In the PD Multi Tier flow (`remote_decoder` / `remote_prefiller`, secondary tier
of `type: p2p`),
a producer that **already holds the requested blocks** supplies nothing to the
consumer. The consumer's fetch demand parks unsatisfied, waits out
`_LOAD_TIMEOUT_S = 30.0`, aborts, and recomputes the prompt locally.

The effect is inverted from the intent: the better the producer's prefix cache
works, the more often the Multi Tier path fails to deliver.

### Environment

- vLLM `v0.27.1`, stock `docker.io/vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1`
- `openai/gpt-oss-120b`, TP=1, `--block-size 128`,
  `--no-disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager`, `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` on all instances
- 2x H200, RDMA between pods
- Connector on both instances:

```
--kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector","kv_role":"kv_both",
  "kv_load_failure_policy":"recompute",
  "kv_connector_extra_config":{"spec_name":"TieringOffloadingSpec",
    "cpu_bytes_to_use":107374182400,"block_size":128,"eviction_policy":"lru",
    "offload_prompt_only":false,
    "secondary_tiers":[{"type":"p2p","host":"$(POD_IP)","port":7777}]}}'
```

Two files (`tiering/p2p/session/server.py`, `.../client.py`) carried added
`logger.info` counters only, no behavioural change; the timings and byte counts
below come from vLLM's own metrics and logs.

### Reproducer

Two instances, A (producer) and B (consumer). No P/D topology, router or proxy
required — three HTTP calls.

1. **Producer leg** on A: `POST /v1/completions`, `max_tokens=1`,
   `kv_transfer_params={"remote_decoder":{"kv_request_id":ID}}`
2. **Consumer leg** on B: `POST /v1/completions`,
   `kv_transfer_params={"remote_prefiller":{"kv_request_id":ID,"remote_host":A,"remote_port":7777}}`

Run that pair twice with a **unique prompt each time** (so the consumer is always
cold). Before the second pair, send the prompt to A once on its own with no
`kv_transfer_params`, so A already holds the blocks.

Prompt ~8K tokens. Watch `vllm:kv_offload_load_bytes_total` on B.

### Observed

| case | producer leg | consumer leg | consumer bytes loaded |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| A cold for the prefix | 0.20 s | 0.16 s | +268,959,744 (256 MiB) |
| A pre-warmed | 0.03 s | **32.9 s** | **0** |

Identical with a real P/D pair (prefill producer, decode consumer):
0.086 s / +256 MiB cold vs 30.2 s / 0 bytes warm. Reproduces every time.

Consumer log for the warm case:

```
P2PSession <A>:7777: <id> round=0 timed out, sending abort
P2PSession <A>:7777: load request <id> (job_id=N) timed out; load job completed
with failure. If this recurs, ensure PYTHONHASHSEED is set to the same value on
all nodes.
```

`PYTHONHASHSEED=0` was set and verified identical on every instance, so that
hint is misleading for this failure mode.

### Analysis

Supply for a PD round can only come from that request's store jobs
(`session/server.py` `_OutboundRequestState.add_stored_blocks`). A warm producer
creates no store job, so demand parked in `demanded`
(`key -> remote_block_idx: blocks peer wants, awaiting supply`) is never matched.

Two gates prevent the blocks from being offered:

1. `distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py` (~L941):

```python
# Skip prefix-hit chunks for block-level policy; for
# request-level, next_stored_chunk_idx stays at 0 so all
# chunks (including hits) are offloaded.
if req_status.offloading_context.policy == OffloadPolicy.BLOCK_LEVEL:
    group_state.next_stored_chunk_idx = num_chunks
```

`P2PTierManager.on_new_request` returns a bare `RequestOffloadingContext()`,
which defaults to `BLOCK_LEVEL`. `grep -c REQUEST_LEVEL` is **0** for every tier
(`p2p`, `fs`, `obj`, `example`) at `v0.27.1` **and on `main`**, so
`request_level_tiers` is always empty and
`TieringOffloadingManager._cascade_existing_blocks_to_request_level_tiers` never
runs.

2. Forcing `REQUEST_LEVEL` for producer-side requests clears gate 1 — verified,
the request then reaches the store path with `next_stored_chunk_idx=0` and 56
storable chunks — but the keys are then dropped by `if block_id == 0: continue`,
since a prefix-hit request has no GPU block ids recorded for those blocks
(measured: 55 keys dropped). `new_offload_keys` empties, `prepare_store` is
skipped, and with it the cascade.

### Why symmetric (non-PD) Multi Tier is unaffected

`session/server.py`:

> `# Supply came from inbound lookup pins (symmetric): no late submit_store can arrive, so unmatched fetch demand fails fast. PD rounds park demand for stores instead.`

`session/client.py`:

> `PD-only loads leave probes/unsent empty ... PD clients never probe and stay on round 0.`

The symmetric path supplies from tier lookups and pins, which need neither a store job
nor GPU block ids, so a warm producer is its best case. PD has no equivalent
route.

### Impact at scale

Shared-prefix workload, 8 producers + 8 consumers, 10,800 requests. Supply match
rate tracks producer cache warmth:

| | cold | warming | warm |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| fetch demand matched | 93.8% | 51.5% | **36.7%** |

6,083 load timeouts were logged against 10,800 requests. End to end this made
PD Multi Tier slower than plain NIXL P/D on the same hardware (1571 s vs
1032 s to completion; mean TPOT 92 ms vs 10.7 ms).

### Question

Should the PD Multi Tier path gain a lookup/pin supply route like the symmetric one, or should
the p2p tier declare `REQUEST_LEVEL` (and the store path then be able to offload
prefix-hit blocks that have no GPU block id)? The second looks like it fights both
the `BLOCK_LEVEL` optimisation and the missing block-id constraint, so the first
seems closer to the existing design — but that is your call.

[Bug]: OffloadingConnector CPU tier leaks its /dev/shm mmap file on any unclean exit (including SIGKILL)

### Your current environment

Used commit: beca88e59ea75a7aa1af72a5ae50188fa91d4e3d
- Wheel: vllm-0.26.1rc1.dev363+gbeca88e59 (nightly dev build from wheels.vllm.ai)
- Version tag: 0.26.1rc1.dev363


### 🐛 Describe the bug

`vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/shared_offload_region.py`'s `SharedOffloadRegion` backs the CPU-tier KV cache with a real tmpfs file at `/dev/shm/vllm_offload_{engine_id}.mmap` (`O_CREAT | O_EXCL`). Nothing removes it automatically - the only cleanup is `SharedOffloadRegion.cleanup()` -> `os.unlink()`, called from one site, `CPUOffloadingWorker.shutdown()`, which is wired into automatic cleanup only via `AsyncLLM.__del__`.

Any exit that skips that destructor leaks the file, it happened when I used vLLM offload within an RL framework that killed the engines unexpectedly but even a regular `SIGKILL` will result in the same thing - it can't be caught by `__del__`, `atexit`, or any signal handler, by kernel design, on any process. Same for embedding the engine as a library that never explicitly calls shutdown before dropping the reference. Each leak is `cpu_bytes_to_use` in size, one per engine instance; repeated restarts (CI, training loops, worker restarts) silently accumulate until `/dev/shm` fills, and the resulting failure (`Insufficient space in /dev/shm`) shows up on a later, unrelated engine start with no link back to cause.

Since /dev/shm is host/pod-wide, not vLLM-private, this doesn't just fail vLLM's own next restart - any other process on the same host or container can draw on, so it can degrade or break unrelated applications too, not only later vLLM runs.

**Reproduced directly:** I easily reproduced it - started a normal engine, confirmed its `vllm_offload_*.mmap` file present in `/dev/shm`, then `kill -9`'d the `VLLM::EngineCore` process. `/dev/shm` usage was unchanged (file still present, same size, process confirmed dead) - a plain `SIGKILL`, no framework involved, reproduces the leak on demand.

**Suggested fix:** unlink-after-rendezvous rather than unlink-on-explicit-shutdown. The file has to stay path-discoverable only long enough for sibling rank processes to attach (`O_CREAT|O_EXCL` creator, others join via `open(path, O_RDWR)`) - once all expected ranks have attached, unlink it. Every rank's already-open fd stays valid; the kernel frees the backing pages once the last fd closes, for any reason at all, no userspace cleanup required after that point. Standard POSIX-shm pattern (`shm_open` + `shm_unlink` once attached), just not applied here yet.

Malformed /v1/responses request returns a >100MB validation-error body (full input echoed per error)

### Summary

A single malformed `POST /v1/responses` request can produce an **HTTP 400 response body over 100 MB**, because the request's entire `input` payload is echoed **once per validation error**. With an input that produces thousands of validation errors, the response size explodes far beyond the request size — a response-amplification / DoS vector against clients and any proxy in front of vLLM.

### Environment

- vLLM `0.23.1rc1.dev601+ga16dbd5b8` (nightly), OpenAI-compatible server, Responses API (`/v1/responses`).
- Served model: `zai-org/GLM-5.2` (FP8), text-only. (The model is incidental — this is server-side request validation, not model behavior.)

### What happens

When an `/v1/responses` request has an `input` whose shape fails Pydantic validation (e.g. `input` given as a list of message-shaped objects where a field has the wrong type), the server returns a 400 whose body is a Pydantic validation-error dump. Each individual error entry **embeds the full offending `input` value** under its `input` key. For a request with N content items that each fail, you get ~N error entries, each carrying a copy of the whole payload.

Observed in production: one such request produced **12,047 validation errors** and a **~114 MB response body** from a request of a few KB. Representative (truncated) error entry:

```
{"type": "string_type", "loc": ("body", "input", "str"), "msg": "Input should be a valid string", "input": [{"type": "message", "role": "user", "content": [{"type": "i... (full input repeated) ...}]}
```

### Impact

- Clients and proxies must buffer/parse a 100 MB+ body for what should be a small 400.
- In our case the downstream proxy (LiteLLM) read and post-processed the entire body, stalling its event loop and inflating memory — a small malformed request cascaded into a service outage. (Filing the proxy-side hardening separately with that project.)

### Expected behavior

A validation error for a malformed request should be **bounded in size**. Options:
- Cap the number of echoed error entries (e.g. first N), and/or
- Omit or truncate the echoed `input` value in each error entry (the field name + type is enough to diagnose), and/or
- Return a single summarized validation error rather than one-per-element.

### Repro sketch

Send `POST /v1/responses` with `input` as a JSON array of ~thousands of message-shaped objects where a field type is invalid for the expected schema, and observe the 400 response body size scale with the element count.

Additional configurations, same script ``` scenario svc disp E2EL sched p99 p99 sched ------------------------------------------------------------------------ 10 req/s, uncapped 500 0 507 507 508 508 10 req/s, concurrency 1 500 1426 506 1932 507 3330 20 req/s, concurrency 8 190 0 197 197 198 198 40 req/s, uncapped 190 0 196 196 198 198 40 req/s, concurrency 4 190 440 196 637 198 1080 inf, uncapped 190 5 214 219 218 220 inf, concurrency 4 190 899 198 1097 200 1998 all times in ms; svc = server service time, disp = mean dispatch delay ``` Every uncapped control comes out at 1.0x, so this is not general client overhead. Ratios were stable to the decimal across three consecutive runs.
#### Cause `limited_request_func` holds the semaphore around the entire request function ([serve.py L975-L979](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/a18dbe49add8adcbf1d9f7b7429e2f249cfc625d/vllm/benchmarks/serve.py#L975-L979)): ```python async def limited_request_func(request_func_input, session, pbar): async with semaphore: return await request_func( request_func_input=request_func_input, session=session, pbar=pbar ) ``` The clock starts inside, at `st = time.perf_counter()`, after the semaphore has been acquired. `TCPConnector` is also limited to `max_concurrency`, but connector-level queueing happens inside `session.post()`, which is after the clock starts, so that part is already captured. The semaphore wait is the only thing excluded. There are four such sites, so this affects generation and pooling backends alike: [`async_request_openai_completions` L198](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/a18dbe49add8adcbf1d9f7b7429e2f249cfc625d/vllm/benchmarks/lib/endpoint_request_func.py#L198-L199), [`async_request_openai_chat_completions` L378](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/a18dbe49add8adcbf1d9f7b7429e2f249cfc625d/vllm/benchmarks/lib/endpoint_request_func.py#L378-L379), [`async_request_openai_audio` L496](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/a18dbe49add8adcbf1d9f7b7429e2f249cfc625d/vllm/benchmarks/lib/endpoint_request_func.py#L496-L497), and [`_run_pooling_request` L593](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/a18dbe49add8adcbf1d9f7b7429e2f249cfc625d/vllm/benchmarks/lib/endpoint_request_func.py#L593-L594). The net effect is that reported tail latency improves as the client falls further behind, which is the failure mode usually associated with coordinated omission in open-loop load generators. #### Related #21108 fixed request-generation drift, which is why the scheduled timestamps are trustworthy today. #45502 identified the same semaphore interaction but addressed load shaping rather than accounting for the wait in the latency numbers, and was closed unmerged. I could not find an issue or PR covering the latency measurement itself. #### Possible direction One additive fix would be to preserve the scheduled arrival timestamp and expose benchmark-side dispatch delay plus schedule-relative latency as separate metrics, leaving the existing TTFT and E2EL definitions and values untouched, with the invariant: ``` schedule_relative_e2el = dispatch_delay + e2el ``` Worth noting that `start_time` should not be redefined to do this, since it already feeds `max_output_tokens_per_s` and `max_concurrent_requests` and is exported as `start_times`. #### Open design question Under `--request-rate inf` every scheduled arrival collapses to the benchmark start, so schedule-relative latency becomes "how long since the run began" rather than a per-request latency. That may still be useful as queue-sojourn behaviour, but calling it latency gets strange. One option is to report these metrics only for finite request rates. Since `inf` is the documented most-common configuration, that choice decides whether the numbers appear in most runs at all, so I would rather settle it before writing the patch. [Bug]: GraniteMoeHybrid cannot load per-expert quantized checkpoints — KeyError: 'layers.0.block_sparse_moe.experts.w2_weight'

### Your current environment

## Summary

`GraniteMoeHybridForCausalLM` cannot load any quantized checkpoint that stores
one tensor per expert (the layout `llm-compressor` emits). Weight loading aborts
with a `KeyError` before the engine reaches inference, so the model is
unservable rather than merely slow or inaccurate.

The MoE expert parameters moved one level down into a `RoutedExperts` submodule
in dc68bd8c4 ([#41184](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41184)). That
commit updated the fused `input_linear` / `output_linear` branch of
`GraniteMoeHybridModel.load_weights()` but not the per-expert quantized branch,
which still resolves pre-refactor parameter names.

## Environment

- Model: `GraniteMoeHybridForCausalLM` (Granite 4 MoE Hybrid)
- Quantization: INT8 W8A8, `compressed-tensors`
- vLLM: source build on `main` at `b3af042ab`
- Platform: CPU. The zentorch plugin is installed but not implicated — the
  failure is in generic weight-name resolution, not in a kernel.

<paste `python collect_env.py` output here>

## Reproduction

Serve any Granite MoE Hybrid checkpoint quantized with per-expert tensors:

```bash
lm_eval --model vllm \
  --model_args pretrained=/path/to/quantized_granite_moe_hybrid,trust_remote_code=True \
  --tasks gsm8k
```

Checkpoint keys follow this pattern for every expert `0..N-1` in every MoE
layer, each `.weight` accompanied by a matching `.weight_scale`:

```
model.layers.0.block_sparse_moe.experts.0.gate_proj.weight
model.layers.0.block_sparse_moe.experts.0.up_proj.weight
model.layers.0.block_sparse_moe.experts.0.down_proj.weight
```

Result:

```
KeyError: 'layers.0.block_sparse_moe.experts.w2_weight'
```

<paste the full traceback here>




### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Root cause

`get_expert_mapping()` in `vllm/model_executor/models/granitemoehybrid.py`
returns pre-refactor destination prefixes:

```python
"block_sparse_moe.experts.w13_"  # gate_proj / up_proj
"block_sparse_moe.experts.w2_"   # down_proj
```

`_load_quant_expert()` applies them with a plain `str.replace`, so the name it
looks up omits the `routed_experts.` level that now exists in the module tree:

| checkpoint key | name after replace | name in `params_dict` |
|---|---|---|
| `experts.0.gate_proj.weight` | `experts.w13_weight` | `experts.routed_experts.w13_weight` |
| `experts.0.up_proj.weight` | `experts.w13_weight` | `experts.routed_experts.w13_weight` |
| `experts.0.down_proj.weight` | `experts.w2_weight` | `experts.routed_experts.w2_weight` |

`params_dict[name_mapped]` then raises. `is_pp_missing_parameter()` runs first
but does not filter these names, so there is no path that swallows the miss.

Two pieces of evidence that this is an incomplete migration rather than an
unsupported checkpoint layout:

1. dc68bd8c4 touched this exact file and spelled out
   `.experts.routed_experts.w13_` / `.experts.routed_experts.w2_` in the fused
   `input_linear` / `output_linear` branch of the same `load_weights()`. Only the
   per-expert branch kept the old names — the two branches now disagree about the
   module layout.
2. The same commit added
   `maybe_remap_moe_expert_param_name()` to `weight_utils.py` as the migration
   shim for precisely this rename, and `llama4.py` / `mllama4.py` already call it
   at their expert-name lookups.

## Proposed fix

Route the mapped name through the existing shim in `_load_quant_expert()`:

```python
from vllm.model_executor.model_loader.weight_utils import (
    maybe_remap_moe_expert_param_name,
)

name_mapped = name.replace(weight_name, param_name)
name_mapped = maybe_remap_moe_expert_param_name(name_mapped, params_dict)
param = params_dict[name_mapped]
```

Resolution becomes:

```
layers.0.block_sparse_moe.experts.0.down_proj.weight
  -> layers.0.block_sparse_moe.experts.w2_weight
  -> layers.0.block_sparse_moe.experts.routed_experts.w2_weight
```

The helper rewrites a name only when it matches a known expert-parameter suffix
*and* the rewritten name exists in `params_dict`, so it is a no-op for any layout
that does not have the `routed_experts` level. `w13_weight_scale` /
`w2_weight_scale` are in that suffix list, so the scale tensors — which reach
`_load_quant_expert()` through the same mapping — are remapped alongside the
weights.

Two alternatives I considered and rejected:

- **Bake `routed_experts` into `get_expert_mapping()`.** Fewer moving parts, but
  it hardcodes the post-refactor layout at a site whose whole purpose is
  checkpoint-name translation, and drops the presence check that keeps other
  layouts loading.
- **Wrap the `weights` iterator in `remap_moe_expert_weights()`, as `gpt_oss.py`
  does.** Covers every branch at once and is the better end state, but it changes
  name resolution for the fused and non-expert branches too, which are already
  correct. That is a refactor with its own test burden, not a fix for this bug;
  worth doing separately if maintainers want the file consistent.

## References

- [#41184](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41184) (dc68bd8c4) — the
  FusedMoE / MoERunner refactor that introduced `routed_experts` and the remap
  helper, and partially updated this file
- [#45818](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/45818) — same class of
  regression in gpt-oss (unquantized path), fixed via
  `remap_moe_expert_weights()`
- [#42463](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42463) /
  [#50037](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50037) — earlier expert
  layout loading work on non-hybrid GraniteMoE. Different model class and a
  different failure; noted only to pre-empt a duplicate flag.
- `vllm/model_executor/models/granitemoehybrid.py` — `get_expert_mapping()`,
  `_load_quant_expert()`
- `vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_utils.py` —
  `maybe_remap_moe_expert_param_name()`, `remap_moe_expert_weights()`

### Before submitting a new issue...

[Bug]: vLLM 0.27.1 declares an unbounded `mcp` dependency but is incompatible with MCP SDK 2.x

### Your current environment

## Environment

- OS: Linux
- Python: 3.12.13
- vLLM: 0.27.1
- MCP SDK: 2.0.0 (problematic) / 1.27.2 (working)
- Model: Qwen3
- GPU: NVIDIA H20 96 GB
- NVIDIA Driver: 580.76.05
- CUDA: 13.0
- Installation: pip


### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Reproduction

#### 1. Install the affected versions

```bash
pip install vllm==0.27.1
pip install mcp==2.0.0
```
#### 2. Start any MCP SSE server

A minimal MCP SSE server exposing one or more standard MCP tools is sufficient.

The MCP server itself is not required to reproduce the API compatibility issue.

The MCP server can be independently verified with the MCP Python client:
```
result = await session.list_tools()
```
and successfully returns valid MCP Tool objects.

#### 3. Start vLLM with MCP tool-server support
```bash
vllm serve <model> \
    --enable-auto-tool-choice \
    --tool-call-parser hermes \
    --tool-server <mcp-server-host>:<port> \
    --port 6008
```
#### 4. Observe the MCP Tool schema

With mcp==2.0.0:
```python
import mcp.types

tool = mcp.types.Tool(
    name="test",
    description="test",
    input_schema={
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {}
    }
)

print(hasattr(tool, "input_schema"))
print(hasattr(tool, "inputSchema"))
```
Output:
```
True
False
```
However, vLLM 0.27.1 accesses:
```
tool.inputSchema
```
in:
```
vllm/entrypoints/mcp/tool_server.py
```
while MCP 2.0.0 exposes:
```
tool.input_schema
```
#### 5. Verify the workaround 
Downgrade the MCP SDK:
```bash
pip install mcp==1.27.2
```
Restart vLLM with the same configuration. The MCP tools are then successfully discovered and the complete MCP tool-calling flow works.

### Root Cause

The issue is caused by an API incompatibility between vLLM 0.27.1 and MCP SDK 2.0.0.

vLLM 0.27.1 accesses the MCP Tool schema using the legacy inputSchema attribute:

tool.inputSchema

However, MCP SDK 2.0.0 exposes the corresponding attribute as:

tool.input_schema

As a result, vLLM 0.27.1 cannot correctly process MCP Tool objects returned by MCP SDK 2.0.0.

More importantly, vLLM 0.27.1 does not enforce  a compatible MCP SDK version constraint in its package dependencies. Therefore, a normal installation can resolve to an MCP SDK version that is incompatible with vLLM's MCP implementation.

This makes the issue a dependency/API compatibility problem rather than an issue with the MCP server itself.

### Expected Behavior

vLLM should either:

Support the MCP SDK versions that can be installed through its declared dependencies; or
Explicitly constrain the MCP SDK dependency to a compatible version range.

For example, if vLLM 0.27.1 is only compatible with MCP SDK versions prior to 2.0.0, its dependency metadata should prevent installation of incompatible versions.

### Actual Behavior

With:

vllm==0.27.1
mcp==2.0.0

the packages can be installed successfully, but the MCP integration fails at runtime because vLLM expects tool.inputSchema, while MCP 2.0.0 provides tool.input_schema.

### Workaround

Downgrading the MCP SDK to a compatible version resolves the issue:

pip install mcp==1.27.2

After restarting vLLM with the same configuration, MCP tools are successfully discovered and the complete MCP tool-calling flow works.

[Bug]: Sentence-Transformers models saved with sentence-transformers>=5.4.0 are silently mis-pooled — compact `1_Pooling/config.json` (`pooling_mode` string) is not parsed, so vLLM falls back to the architecture-default pooler ` ### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ``` ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug ### Summary When a Sentence-Transformers (ST) model is serialized with **`sentence-transformers>=5.4.0`**, vLLM serves it with the **wrong pooling** and produces incorrect embeddings **with no warning or error**. ST changed the on-disk schema of `1_Pooling/config.json` in **v5.4.0** (commit `29dcd28a`, PR [UKPLab/sentence-transformers#3554](https://github.com/UKPLab/sentence-transformers/pull/3554)): ```jsonc // OLD ("verbose"), sentence-transformers <= 5.3.0 { "word_embedding_dimension": 768, "pooling_mode_cls_token": false, "pooling_mode_mean_tokens": true, "pooling_mode_max_tokens": false, "pooling_mode_mean_sqrt_len_tokens": false, "pooling_mode_weightedmean_tokens": false, "pooling_mode_lasttoken": false, "include_prompt": true } // NEW ("compact"), sentence-transformers >= 5.4.0 { "embedding_dimension": 768, "pooling_mode": "mean", "include_prompt": true } ``` vLLM's `get_pooling_config()` in `vllm/transformers_utils/config.py` only recognizes the **verbose boolean** form. It iterates the pooling dict looking for a key whose value is `True` (`parse_pooling_type` then strips the `pooling_mode_` prefix). The compact schema has **no boolean-valued keys**, so `get_pooling_config()` derives nothing and vLLM silently falls back to the model architecture's **default** pooler: - encoder / BERT-style → **CLS** - decoder-style (Gemma3, Qwen3, …) → **LAST** For any model whose correct pooling differs from that architecture default — e.g. **mean-pooled** BERT sentence encoders, or **mean + Dense** models such as `google/embeddinggemma-300m` — the served embeddings are wrong. There is **no warning**, so the failure is silent. (Separately, for ST models that have `2_Dense`/`3_Dense` projection modules, those Dense layers also appear **not** to be applied when the config is compact — see the embeddinggemma row below.) ### Why this is easy to miss Public HF Hub embedding repos (e.g. `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, `BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5`) still ship the **verbose** `1_Pooling/config.json` and have not been re-saved, so serving the original repos works fine. The compact schema only appears when a model is **re-serialized** through a modern ST — which is exactly what `mlflow.sentence_transformers.log_model()` does (it re-saves the model using whatever ST version is installed). So the breakage shows up on re-serialization pipelines, not on the common "serve the original repo" path. ### Minimal reproduction (public models only) ```bash pip install "sentence-transformers>=5.4.0" python - <<'PY' from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer # all-MiniLM-L6-v2 uses MEAN pooling; original repo ships a VERBOSE config, # but re-saving under ST>=5.4.0 writes the COMPACT schema. m = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2") m.save("/tmp/minilm-st54") PY cat /tmp/minilm-st54/1_Pooling/config.json # -> {"embedding_dimension":384,"pooling_mode":"mean","include_prompt":...} # serve and compare to the sentence-transformers library vllm serve /tmp/minilm-st54 --runner pooling --served-model-name emb ``` Then compare the server's `/v1/embeddings` output against `SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2").encode(...)`. Because vLLM uses CLS (architecture default) instead of MEAN, the per-sentence cosine similarity is well below 1.0. ### Evidence (server output vs. the `sentence-transformers` library, cosine per sentence) Tested on vLLM **0.23.0**, CPU backend, `--runner pooling`, bf16. "auto" = no `--pooler-config`. | model | required pooling | config schema | vLLM resolved pooler | cosine vs ST lib | |---|---|---|---|---| | mean-pooled BERT (e.g. all-MiniLM / ko-sbert) | MEAN | compact (ST 5.6) | **CLS** (arch default) | **~0.89** ❌ | | same model | MEAN | compact + `--pooler-config '{"pooling_type":"MEAN"}'` | MEAN | **1.0000** ✅ | | same model | MEAN | **verbose (ST 5.3)** | MEAN (auto) | **1.0000** ✅ | | Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B | LAST | compact | LAST (arch default) | **0.9998** ✅ *(only correct by coincidence — arch default == required)* | | embeddinggemma-300m (mean + Dense) | MEAN + Dense | compact | LAST (arch default) | **~0.02** ❌ | | embeddinggemma-300m | MEAN + Dense | compact + `--pooler-config '{"pooling_type":"MEAN"}'` | MEAN | **~0.01** ❌ *(pooling fixed but Dense still not applied)* | | embeddinggemma-300m | MEAN + Dense | **verbose (ST 5.3)** | MEAN (auto) + Dense applied | **0.9999** ✅ | Key points: - With a **verbose** config, vLLM auto-detects the correct pooling (and applies the Dense projector) for all three → cosine ~1.0. - With a **compact** config, vLLM silently uses the architecture default. It happens to be correct for decoder embedders that genuinely use LAST (Qwen3-Embedding), which **masks** the bug, but is wrong for mean-pooled encoders and for mean+Dense models. - For embeddinggemma, forcing `--pooler-config '{"pooling_type":"MEAN"}'` fixes the pooling but the output is still orthogonal to the ST library, suggesting the `2_Dense`/`3_Dense` projector is not applied in the compact-config path either. ### Suggested fix In `get_pooling_config()` (`vllm/transformers_utils/config.py`): 1. **Parse the compact schema too.** If `1_Pooling/config.json` contains a string `pooling_mode` key, map it to the pooling type: `cls → CLS`, `mean → MEAN`, `max → MAX`, `lasttoken → LAST`, `weightedmean → …`, `mean_sqrt_len_tokens → …`. (This mirrors ST's own load-side `config_key_renames` / legacy-kwargs conversion, which already handles both directions internally.) 2. **Don't fail silently.** If a `1_Pooling/config.json` is present but no pooling type can be derived, emit a warning instead of quietly falling back to the architecture default — that single warning would have surfaced this immediately. 3. Confirm the ST Dense projector (`_load_st_projector` / `try_get_dense_modules` in `vllm/model_executor/models/adapters.py`) is engaged for these models regardless of the `1_Pooling` schema version (embeddinggemma row above). ### Related - #9388 / #9506 — the feature that introduced sentence-transformers config parsing (verbose boolean form only; predates the ST 5.4.0 compact schema). - #15929 — a model-specific "should use mean pooling" report (same class of wrong-default-pooling symptom). - ST schema change: UKPLab/sentence-transformers PR #3554, first released in v5.4.0. ### Before submitting - [x] Searched existing issues/PRs (no existing report of the compact `1_Pooling/config.json` schema not being parsed; closest are #9388 and #15929). - [x] Reproducible on the latest release (0.23.0). ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

### 🐛 Describe the bug ## Summary When generation terminates (via `max_tokens`/`length` **or** a `stop` string) while the streaming parser engine is inside a **`` opener that has not yet been promoted to a tool call** (i.e. the function name has not been parsed), the streaming response **drops the buffered markup**, while the non-streaming response **returns it as `content`**. The two paths disagree for the same input. This is in the new `ParserEngine` path (PR #45413), exercised by `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder` / `qwen3_xml`. It is independent of #42210 (which is the legacy `ToolParser` path). ## Environment - vLLM `0.23.1rc1.dev608+gfb42e5219` (current `main`) - Model: `Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B`, `--enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3` - `temperature: 0` (deterministic) ## Reproduction (live server, deterministic) ``` vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B \ --tensor-parallel-size 2 \ --port 8001 \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --stream-interval 251 ``` ### A. Cleanest repro — `length` cutoff, reasoning disabled Send the same request with `"stream": false` then `"stream": true`, sweeping `max_tokens`. `chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": false}` makes the model emit the tool call immediately so the cutoff lands in the opener: ```bash curl -s http://localhost:8001/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{ "model": "Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B", "stream": true, "temperature": 0.0, "max_tokens": 4, "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in San Francisco?"}], "tools": [{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_weather","description":"Get weather for a location","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"location":{"type":"string"}},"required":["location"]}}}] }' ``` | `max_tokens` | non-streaming `content` | streaming `content` | result | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | `""` | `null` | **DIVERGE** | | 2 | `"\n"` | `null` | **DIVERGE** | | 3 | `"\n<"` | `null` | **DIVERGE** | | 4 | `"\n= 5` the function name is parseable and both paths emit a `tool_calls` delta (match). ### B. Same bug with reasoning ENABLED (not an artifact of disabling thinking) With the default thinking on, the model reasons first (~115 tokens here), so the cutoff hits the opener at a higher, narrower `max_tokens` window: | `max_tokens` (thinking on) | non-streaming `content` | streaming `content` | result | |---|---|---|---| | ≤114 | `null` (cutoff in reasoning) | `null` | match | | 116 | `"\n\n"` | `null` | **DIVERGE** | | 118 | `"\n\n\n<"` | `null` | **DIVERGE** | | ≥120 | `null` (+`tool_calls`) | `null` (+`tool_calls`) | match | (Reasoning content itself is consistent across both paths; only the un-promoted tool opener diverges.) ### C. Also reproduces with `stop` strings | stop string | `include_stop_str_in_output` | non-streaming `content` | streaming `content` | result | |---|---|---|---|---| | `"\n\n"` | `null` | **DIVERGE** | | `"\n", add_special_tokens=False) def stream(n): p = PCls(tok, []); out = "" for k in range(n): piece = tok.decode([ids[k]]) dm = p.parse_delta(delta_text=piece, delta_token_ids=[ids[k]], request=req, prompt_token_ids=[1], finished=(k == n - 1)) if dm and dm.content: out += dm.content return out for n in (2, 3, 4): text = tok.decode(ids[:n]) ns = PCls(tok, []).parse(text, req, enable_auto_tools=True)[1] print(n, repr(text), "stream=", repr(stream(n)), "nonstream=", repr(ns)) # 2 '\n' stream= '' nonstream= '\n' # 3 '\n<' stream= '' nonstream= '\n<' # 4 '\n` fires `TOOL_CALL_START` immediately (`tool_index = 0`, `vllm/parser/qwen3.py`), so the buffered text is in a tool state with no client-visible delta yet. - `TOOL_PREAMBLE` text has no `content_events` entry, so it is dropped in `StreamingParserEngine._emit_for_state`; the opener terminals are consumed by transitions with no content event. - `StreamingParserEngine.finish()` emits `TOOL_CALL_END` (since `tool_index >= 0`) but never re-emits the consumed opener as content. - Non-streaming (`DelegatingParser.parse` → `_extract_tool_calls`) returns the original `content` (the raw markup) when no complete tool call is found. ## Notes / scope - Direction (A) at the engine layer is fragile: it conflicts with the existing test `tests/parser/engine/test_engine.py::TestToolPreambleFinish::test_finish_emits_tool_call_end_with_tool_index` (which asserts `TOOL_CALL_END` for an opened-but-empty call), and it over-flushes when the opener *is* a stop string (e.g. `stop=[""]`, where non-streaming strips it). The engine cannot see stop-stripping. - Direction (B) is a small change in `DelegatingParser._extract_tool_calls` (return the tool parser's content, which already drops incomplete markup) and is contained, but it changes shared non-streaming behavior across all parsers. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

+    markers. Inkling has none — ``<|end_message|>`` is labelled THINK_END

[Bug]: stack overflow causing system crash: Rust unbounded recursion in the Gemma4 unified parser

### Your current environment

vllm/collect_env.py output is not included: this reproduces entirely against the Rust workspace under rust/, driven by cargo test and the in-tree mock engine. The vLLM Python package is not installed on the repro machine and there is no GPU, so collect_env.py would report N/A for essentially every field it exists to collect. Nothing in the affected code path touches torch, CUDA, or the Python runtime. Happy to provide a full collect_env.py dump from a GPU install if that is needed for triage.
<details>

<summary>A rust frontend issue, GPU not required</summary>

```text
Your output of `python collect_env.py` here
```

</details>


### 🐛 Describe the bug

When fuzzing, I found that`Gemma4UnifiedParser` parses tool-call arguments with a **_recursive-descent grammar that has no depth limit._** 

Assistant output containing deeply nested `{`/`[` inside a tool call recurses until the thread's stack is exhausted. A Rust stack overflow is not a catchable panic. the runtime prints `fatal runtime error: stack overflow` and aborts the process immediately. Roughly **6 KB of generated text is enough** on a 2 MiB stack (tokio's default worker stack size), which, I argue is an ordinary response length :)



- **Component:** `rust/src/parser/src/unified/gemma4.rs`
- **Tested at commit:** `e2fa28594f7baad142a426b0b6a2cfe2c79201c7`
- **Precondition:** serving a model configured to use the `gemma4` unified parser.
- **Vector:** model output, which a user can attempt to steer through prompt content.

## Reproduction
use this `gemma4_stack_overflow.rs` file: https://gist.github.com/Yunzez/8e98d656aa667095b513161eb056d28e


The attached `gemma4_stack_overflow.rs` is a single self-contained example. Drop it into your checkout and run:

```bash
mkdir -p rust/src/parser/examples          # make dir for repro
cp gemma4_stack_overflow.rs rust/src/parser/examples/
cd rust

# (a) Default 8 MiB main-thread stack — needs nesting depth 6000 (24 KB of text).
cargo run --release -p vllm-parser --example gemma4_stack_overflow
#   thread 'main' has overflowed its stack
#   fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting

# (b) 2 MiB stack, matching tokio's default worker — depth 1500 (6 KB).
#     This is the size that matters for the server; a single-threaded reproducer
#     needs the smaller ulimit to show it.
ulimit -s 2048
cargo run --release -p vllm-parser --example gemma4_stack_overflow 1500
#   thread 'main' has overflowed its stack
#   fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting
```

**Run the matching stack size and depth or it will not reproduce**, depth 1500 is harmless on an 8 MiB stack. The example takes the depth as its only argument (default 6000) and builds the payload itself:

```
<|tool_call>call:f  +  "{a:" * depth  +  "1"  +  "}" * depth  +  <tool_call|>
```

### Measured thresholds

Depth is the nesting level; bytes is the whole payload.

| Stack | Depth 1200 | Depth 1500 | Depth 5000 | Depth 6000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 MiB (`ulimit -s 2048`, tokio worker default) | ok (1.6 ms) | **overflow** | **overflow** | **overflow** |
| 8 MiB (default main thread) | ok (1.7 ms) | ok (2.1 ms) | ok (7.8 ms) | **overflow** |

So the payload needed is ~6 KB against a tokio worker and ~24 KB against an 8 MiB stack. Note the *time* is milliseconds right up to the cliff, this is not a slow degradation that a timeout would catch, it is fast until it aborts.

## Root cause

The value grammar is mutually recursive with no depth accounting (`rust/src/parser/src/unified/gemma4.rs`)

### Scope: Gemma4 is the only parser affected

I checked the rest of the crate rather than leaving this as a guess. `gemma4.rs` is the **only** parser with a hand-written recursive bracket grammar. a search for the recursion sites across `src/parser/src` returns just two hits.

SimpleCPUOffloadConnector (eager): stored blocks never registered in hash map (lookup always misses) + requests finish with ~44% of blocks never stored (TODO: flush on finish)

# SimpleCPUOffloadConnector (eager mode): stored CPU blocks are never discoverable by lookup, and requests finish with ~44% of blocks never stored

## Summary

While using `VLLM_USE_SIMPLE_KV_OFFLOAD=1` (SimpleCPUOffloadConnector, eager mode) with prefix caching enabled, we found two bugs in `vllm/v1/simple_kv_offload/manager.py` (both present on current `main`):

1. **CPU-side blocks are never registered in the hash map** — stores stamp `cpu_blk._block_hash = bhash` directly, bypassing `BlockPool._insert_block_hash()`, so `cached_block_hash_to_block` never gains an entry. Every lookup misses. `vllm:external_prefix_cache_hits_total` stays at 0 forever while `kv_offload_store_bytes_total` keeps growing.

2. **Requests finish with a large fraction of confirmed blocks never stored** (the known `TODO: flush on finish.` at manager.py:534, but the gap is much larger than "one block"): during prefill the eager scan stores ~`sched_tokens/block_size` blocks per step, but once the request transitions to decode, `yield_req_data` stops reporting the accumulated blocks and nothing ever walks the remaining backlog. On a 185K-token prompt with `--max-num-batched-tokens 4096`, only 112 of 217 blocks (52%) reached the CPU pool by the time the request finished.

## Root cause analysis

### Bug 1: bare hash assignment (manager.py:518 and :642)

```python
for cpu_blk, bhash in zip(cpu_blocks_alloc, block_hashes_to_store):
    cpu_blk._block_hash = bhash  # type: ignore[assignment]
```

The lookup path (`get_num_new_matched_tokens` → `cpu_coordinator.find_longest_cache_hit` → `BlockPool.get_cached_block` → `cached_block_hash_to_block.get_one_block(...)`) only consults the hash map. Setting the attribute on the block object is not visible to it. The P2P tier manager in the same tree registers via the proper primitive.

Fix: use `cpu_block_pool._insert_block_hash(bhash, cpu_blk, num_tokens=None)`. If `hash_block_size < block_size` (fine-grained hashing, e.g. `prefix_match_unit=8`), the GPU block's full hash set (`cached_block_hashes_by_block`) must be migrated too, or lookups at hash granularity still miss.

### Bug 2: no final flush of the store backlog at request finish

Observed with a 185K-token request (block_size=1648, chunked prefill):

```
REQFIN prompt=185023 computed=185033 state_blocks=217 stored_cursor=112
```

`state.num_stored_blocks` had reached only 112 of 217 blocks when the request finished. After `request_finished()`, the per-request store state is cleaned up and the backlog is never stored — those blocks are only recoverable by full recompute.

Fix sketch (we run this in production): in `request_finished_all_groups()` — **before** `request_finished()` cleans up, and while the blocks still hold their request references — walk the scheduler-provided authoritative block list (`block_ids` argument, from `kv_cache_manager.get_block_ids_for_computed_tokens`) from `num_stored_blocks` to `aligned_tokens // g_block_size`, and submit the remainder as one final store event. The event must be carried to the worker by the *next* `build_connector_meta()` (we add a `sent` flag on `TransferMeta` and merge unsent events into the next batch).

## Reproduction

Environment: 2x RTX 3090, vLLM 0.26.1rc1 custom build, Qwen3.5-hybrid (Mamba + SWA + full attention groups), `--enable-prefix-caching --kv-offloading-size 60 --kv-offloading-backend native`, `VLLM_USE_SIMPLE_KV_OFFLOAD=1`.

Reproducer (same 40K-token prompt sent twice, cold):

```python
# request 1: cold prefill (~27s)
# request 2: expected CPU hit after GPU eviction, observed full recompute
import json, time, urllib.request
# ... send identical prompt twice, compare vllm:external_prefix_cache_hits_total delta (0 before fix)
```

After both fixes (measured on our deployment):
- 40K prompt, blocks evicted from GPU by unrelated traffic: second call drops from ~27s (full recompute) to 1.8s (CPU load hit)
- 2x 148K sessions rotating on a 291K-token GPU pool: alternating calls recover in 4.3-4.5s with 98% external hit rate (145,024 / 148,022 tokens), vs. 62s partial-hit before the flush fix

## Additional notes

- The TODO comment at manager.py:534 acknowledges the "last full block" case; in practice the backlog is far larger (48% in our measurements) because nothing walks the backlog during decode.
- Happy to upstream both fixes as PRs with unit tests if the analysis is confirmed — the fixes have been running in production for us.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Description of the bug

Streaming tool calls (`stream: true`) on DeepSeek-V4-Pro with the `deepseek_v4` tool call parser leak raw DSML markup into tool call arguments. Non-streaming mode works correctly.

## Reproduction

### Hosted
```python
import json, requests

BASE = "http://<server>:8000/v1"
MODEL = "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro"

tools = [{
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "get_weather",
        "description": "Get weather for a location",
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "location": {"type": "string"},
                "date": {"type": "string"}
            },
            "required": ["location"]
        }
    }
}]

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Paris and Tokyo tomorrow?"}]

resp = requests.post(f"{BASE}/chat/completions", json={
    "model": MODEL,
    "messages": messages,
    "tools": tools,
    "tool_choice": "required",
    "stream": True,
}, stream=True, timeout=120)

for line in resp.iter_lines():
    if not line: continue
    line = line.decode("utf-8")
    if line.startswith("data: "):
        data = line[6:]
        if data == "[DONE]": break
        chunk = json.loads(data)
        delta = chunk["choices"][0].get("delta", {})
        if delta.get("tool_calls"):
            print(json.dumps(delta["tool_calls"]))
```
**Expected**: clean argument deltas like `{"location": "Paris"}`

**Actual**: DSML markup leaks into arguments:
```json
{"tool_calls": [{"index": 0, "function": {"arguments": "{\"location\": \""}}]}
{"tool_calls": [{"index": 0, "function": {"arguments": "Paris</\uff5cDSML\uff5cparameter"}}]}
{"tool_calls": [{"index": 0, "function": {"arguments": "\", \"date\": \""}}]}
```
### Regex-level reproduction (no model, GPU, or server required)

```python
import re, json

_DSML = "｜DSML｜"
_ESCAPED_DSML = re.escape(_DSML)

_PARAM_RE = re.compile(
    rf'<{_ESCAPED_DSML}parameter\s+name="([^"]+)"\s+string="(true|false)">'
    rf"(.*?)</{_ESCAPED_DSML}parameter>",
    re.DOTALL,
)
_PARTIAL_PARAM_RE = re.compile(
    rf'<{_ESCAPED_DSML}parameter\s+name="([^"]+)"\s+string="(true|false)">'
    rf"(.*)$",
    re.DOTALL,
)

def _dsml_arg_converter(raw_args, partial):
    params = {}
    last_end = 0
    for m in _PARAM_RE.finditer(raw_args):
        name, is_str, value = m.group(1), m.group(2), m.group(3)
        params[name] = value if is_str == "true" else value
        last_end = m.end()
    if partial:
        pm = _PARTIAL_PARAM_RE.search(raw_args, last_end)
        if pm:
            params[pm.group(1)] = pm.group(3)
    return json.dumps(params, ensure_ascii=False)

# slot.args with a partial closing tag (missing final >)
raw = "<｜DSML｜parameter name=\"location\" string=\"true\">Paris</｜DSML｜parameter"
print(_dsml_arg_converter(raw, partial=True))
# Output: {"location": "Paris</｜DSML｜parameter"}
# Expected: {"location": "Paris"}
```
## Possible root cause

PR #45877 (commit `fb5291b35b`, July 3 2026) ported DeepSeek V4 from the hand-written `DeepSeekV32ToolParser` to the generic `StreamingParserEngine` framework. The new code introduced `_PARTIAL_PARAM_RE` with `(.*)$` to capture in-progress parameter values during streaming.

## Impact

- `stream: true` with `tool_choice: required`: DSML markup leaks into argument JSON
- `stream: true` with `tool_choice: auto`: tool calls emitted with empty `{}` arguments (no arg deltas streamed)
- `stream: false`: works correctly (unaffected)
- Agent harnesses (e.g. opencode, Claude Code) that use streaming mode fail to execute tool calls

## Proposed fix

Change `_PARTIAL_PARAM_RE` to use a negative lookahead that stops at DSML tag prefixes instead of greedily capturing everything:

```python
_PARTIAL_PARAM_RE = re.compile(
    rf'<{_ESCAPED_DSML}parameter\s+name="([^"]+)"\s+string="(true|false)">'
    rf"((?:(?!</?{_ESCAPED_DSML}).)*)",
    re.DOTALL,
)
```

Root-caused this and opened #53405.

The partial-parameter matcher `_PARTIAL_PARAM_RE` in `vllm/parser/deepseek_v4.py` (introduced in #45877) captures the in-progress value with a greedy `(.*)$`. When streaming stops mid-closing-tag, the truncated fragment is captured verbatim:

```
raw:  <｜DSML｜parameter name="location" string="true">Paris</｜DSML｜parameter
out:  {"location": "Paris</｜DSML｜parameter"}
```

One note on the suggested fix in the issue description: a tempered pattern like `(?:(?!</?｜DSML｜).)*` only stops when the full `｜DSML｜` sequence is visible, but chunk boundaries can land earlier — a value ending in `y</｜DSM` still leaks with that approach (verified experimentally). The PR instead trims the value at the earliest offset where its remainder is a prefix of a DSML tag (`</｜DSML｜parameter>` or `<｜DSML`), which handles truncation at every position inside the tag while leaving ordinary angle brackets in values (`a<b`) untouched.
